Plank theorems and their applications: a survey

William Verreault
Abstract

Plank problems concern the covering of convex bodies by planks in Euclidean space and are related to famous open problems in convex geometry. In this survey, we introduce plank problems and present surprising applications of plank theorems in various areas of mathematics.

1 Introduction

Questions about the covering of convex bodies by planks in Euclidean space are referred to as plank problems in convex geometry and discrete geometry. Here is a toy plank problem.

Question 1.1.

Given a circular table of diameter dd and planks of width 11 and length at least dd, what is the minimal number of planks needed to cover the table?

It is readily seen that we may use dd parallel planks, but can we do better by changing their orientation and by overlapping them if needed? The answer is no. In fact, we will see that even if we consider a countable family of planks of positive and varying widths, it is impossible to cover the table in a way such that the sum of the widths of the planks used is less than dd. Accordingly, a covering by parallel planks is optimal. Alfred Tarski generalized this question in the 1930s, a period when discrete geometry was still nascent, and what became known as Tarski’s plank problem is still the source of numerous problems and conjectures in geometry despite having been solved decades ago.

This survey covers a few plank problems and plank theorems and presents various applications of these theorems and the ideas behind their proofs in different fields of mathematics. It is organized as follows. Tarski’s plank problem is described in Section 2. A solution and a generalization from Thøger Bang, as well as an important result called Bang’s lemma, are also included in this section. We present a famous plank theorem of Keith Ball for Banach spaces in Section 3, which proves a specific but important case of Bang’s conjecture. In Section 4, we move on to discussing different ways to strengthen Bang’s lemma and Ball’s plank theorem, as well as several other types of plank problems: spherical and discrete variants, and plank problems on complex Hilbert spaces and Lp​(μ)L_{p}(\mu) spaces. We also present a recent polynomial approach to plank coverings, which is based on general results regarding the zeros of polynomials restricted to the unit sphere and which has been used to obtain streamlined demonstrations of some plank theorems. We then highlight the connection between plank problems and diverse fundamental concepts in analysis and number theory in Sections 5 and 6. The reader can refer to the Table of Contents for a more thorough description of the applications.

This survey is by no means exhaustive, the aim of this paper being first and foremost to present the main ideas and applications of plank theorems. The author still tried to include the major parts of the history behind these problems as well as many details in the proofs of the important results for completeness and an easy access to all readers; the main reason for this being that there is no recent comprehensive survey on plank problems, except possibly [46] whose focus on Tarski’s plank problem is very brief. Anyone familiar with plank theorems is invited to skip over to the applications.

1.1 Notation and conventions

Unless stated otherwise, we work in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and it is always assumed that d≥2d\geq 2. The letter CC will denote a dd-dimensional convex body, that is, a compact convex subset of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with nonempty interior, while HH will denote a hyperplane in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, that is, an affine subspace of dimension d−1d-1.

We recall a few standard definitions needed to properly state and understand plank problems. A (closed) plank PP in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} is the closed set of points between two parallel hyperplanes that are called the boundary hyperplanes of PP. We say that a hyperplane supports a convex body C⊂ℝdC\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} if CC is entirely contained in one of the half-spaces bounded by the hyperplane and the boundary of CC touches the hyperplane in at least one point. Once we fix a direction, we can talk about the hyperplanes that support CC (in the given direction) without ambiguity. Finally, we say that planks P1,P2,…,PnP_{1},P_{2},\ldots,P_{n} cover CC if C⊆⋃i=1nPiC\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}P_{i}. In most problems we shall encounter, it does not matter that the number of planks be finite or countable, but we will assume that it is finite for simplicity’s sake. We refer to the planks PiP_{i} as a covering of CC. The width w⁡(P)w(P) of a plank PP is the distance between the two boundary hyperplanes of PP. We sometimes refer to the sum of the widths of a covering of a convex body as the total width of the covering or of the associated planks. Given a hyperplane HH, the width w⁡(C,H)w(C,H) of a convex body CC in the direction of HH is the distance between the two hyperplanes that support CC and that are parallel to HH. We also define the minimal width w⁡(C)w(C) of a convex body CC as the infimum of w⁡(C,H)w(C,H) over all hyperplanes H⊂ℝdH\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}.

2 Tarski’s plank problem

2.1 The genesis of plank problems

In the 1930s, the mathematician and logician Alfred Tarski, who is known for his work on model theory and the Banach–Tarski paradox, among other things, proposed a problem that would change the face of discrete geometry. It is what we now call a plank problem.

Tarski’s plank problem.

If C⊂ℝdC\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} is covered by a sequence of planks P1,P2​…,PnP_{1},P_{2}\ldots,P_{n}, then the sum of the widths of the planks is at least w⁡(C)w(C).

Without loss of generality, we may consider a body of minimal width 11. Then, similarly to our answer to Question 1.1, it is obvious that we can cover a convex body of minimal width 11 with planks that have total width 11, by placing a family of parallel planks perpendicular to a pair of supporting hyperplanes that realize the minimal width. But can we do better? Tarski’s plank problem says no.

2.1.1 Partial solution to Tarski’s problem

While the statement of the plank problem above never explicitly appeared in Tarski’s work, Bang attributed the two-dimensional version of this conjecture to Tarski in [18]. In fact, Tarski proved his conjecture for figures for which the width equals the diameter of the largest inscribed disk [87]. While this applies to figures like disks and parallelograms, as observed by Tarski, the case of ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} is not entirely covered by this partial result, since some convex figures, for example an equilateral triangle, have a width bigger than the diameter of their inscribed circle; yet, Tarski’s arguments generalize to three-dimensional solids whose width equals the diameter of the largest inscribed ball. However, they do not work in higher dimensions because the proof relies on geometric characteristics of two (or three)-dimensional spaces. His proof is still interesting in its own right, so we include it by adapting the argument that was presented in [62]. Note that Tarski was inspired by a solution of Moese [70] on a related problem first stated by Tarksi himself (read [69, Chapter 7] for a discussion on the history of this problem and a translation of the related papers of Tarski and Moese).

The demonstration relies essentially on a result of Archimedes in On the Sphere and Cylinder, often called “Archimedes’ Hat-Box Theorem”, which can be formulated as follows.

Proposition 2.1.

The lateral area of a spherical segment formed by the intersection of a sphere of radius rr with the region between two parallel hyperplanes separated by distance dd, both of which intersect the sphere, is 2​π​r​d2\pi rd.

We can now use Archimedes’ result to outline Tarski’s argument.

Proof of a special case of Tarski’s problem.

Let DD and BB denote the disk and the sphere of radius rr centered at the origin, respectively. Suppose that planks P1,P2,…,PnP_{1},P_{2},\ldots,P_{n} cover DD and that each plank is entirely contained in DD (replacing PiP_{i} with Pi∩DP_{i}\cap D if needed). Then, the union of the vertical projections of the planks on BB covers the surface of BB, which has area 4​π​r24\pi r^{2}. Thus, the sum of the lateral areas of the spherical segments formed by the intersection of the vertical projections of the PiP_{i} with BB is at least 4​π​r24\pi r^{2}. By Proposition 2.1, it follows that

∑i=1n2​π​r​w​(Pi)≥4​π​r2,\sum_{i=1}^{n}2\pi rw(P_{i})\geq 4\pi r^{2},

whence ∑i=1nw⁡(Pi)≥2​r=w⁡(D)\sum_{i=1}^{n}w(P_{i})\geq 2r=w(D). ∎

2.2 Bang’s solution and conjecture

In 1950, Bang [18] gave an unexpectedly short proof of Tarski’s conjecture. His solution relies heavily on simple geometric ideas, but they are hiding the combinatorial dimension of the argument. The basic ideas behind the proof are still at the core of many demonstrations in convex geometry and discrete geometry, which we shall partly explore in Sections 4 to 6. One year later, Bang [19] simplified his proof and Fenchel [48] simplified it some more. Finally in 1964, Bognár [35] reformulated the demonstration of Fenchel. Bognár’s trick of reducing the statement to the case of centered planks is still sometimes used to simplify plank problems (see Section 2.2.2).

Theorem 2.2.

Let C⊂ℝdC\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a convex body covered by nn planks PjP_{j}, j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n. Then w⁡(P1)+⋯+w⁡(Pn)≥w⁡(C){w(P_{1})+\cdots+w(P_{n})\geq w(C)}.

The proof we include here mostly follows another reformulation [74], but it is more detailed and also presents the end of the demonstration in terms of the important Bang lemma, which will be used extensively in the rest of this paper.

2.2.1 A solution to Tarski’s plank problem

In what follows, we let aj=w⁡(Pj)/2a_{j}=w(P_{j})/2 and we use uju_{j} to denote a vector of length aja_{j} that is perpendicular to the boundary hyperplanes of PjP_{j} (sometimes called the width vector of PjP_{j}). The whole proof essentially relies on two lemmas and then proceeds by contradiction. Here is the first lemma.

Lemma 2.3.

Let uu be a vector of norm a/2a/2 with a<w⁡(C)a<w(C), and let mm be the midpoint of a longest chord in CC parallel to uu (if several longest chords exist, pick any one of them). Then, the intersection (C−u)∩(C+u)(C-u)\cap(C+u) contains a homothetic image of CC with center of homothety mm and homothety ratio κ=(w⁡(C)−a)/w⁡(C)\kappa=(w(C)-a)/w(C).

In the above, C±uC\pm u is the translation of CC by the vector ±u\pm u. As this is a simple geometric statement, one may be convinced of its veracity by looking at Fig. 3. We still give a full proof below for completeness. Also, if the longest chord that is parallel to uu is not unique, the midpoint mm is not uniquely determined, but the lemma holds for any such choice of chord, and the subsequent corollaries only need this type of existence statement.

Proof of Lemma 2.3.

Let the chosen longest chord in CC parallel to uu have endpoints yy and zz, and length ℓ\ell. (If there are several longest chords parallel to uu, choose any one; the argument below does not change.) Under these hypotheses, we may write u=a⁡(z−y)/2​ℓu=a(z-y)/2\ell. If x∈Cx\in C, then the point

aℓ​m+ℓ−aℓ​x+u=aℓ​y+z2+ℓ−aℓ​x+a2​z−yℓ=aℓ​z+ℓ−aℓ​x\frac{a}{\ell}m+\frac{\ell-a}{\ell}x+u=\frac{a}{\ell}\frac{y+z}{2}+\frac{\ell-a}{\ell}x+\frac{a}{2}\frac{z-y}{\ell}=\frac{a}{\ell}z+\frac{\ell-a}{\ell}x

is in CC, since a/ℓ+(ℓ−a)/ℓ=1a/\ell+(\ell-a)/\ell=1 and CC is convex. The same reasoning shows that aℓ​m+ℓ−aℓ​x−u\displaystyle\frac{a}{\ell}m+\frac{\ell-a}{\ell}x-u is also in CC, whence

aℓ​m+ℓ−aℓ​x∈(C−u)∩(C+u).\frac{a}{\ell}m+\frac{\ell-a}{\ell}x\in(C-u)\cap(C+u).

Under the homothety of center mm and ratio (ℓ−a)/ℓ(\ell-a)/\ell, the convex body CC is contracted and covered by the set of points of the form aℓ​m+ℓ−aℓ​x.\displaystyle\frac{a}{\ell}m+\frac{\ell-a}{\ell}x. We conclude that the image of CC under this homothety is contained in (C−u)∩(C+u)(C-u)\cap(C+u).

Let us now compare ℓ\ell and w⁡(C)w(C). There exist supporting hyperplanes to CC at yy and zz whose normals are parallel to the chord direction z−yz-y, else we could move the chord to obtain a bigger one, contradicting maximality. Since the minimal length of CC is defined as the infimum over the distance between such hyperplanes, we must have ℓ≥w⁡(C)\ell\geq w(C). It follows that (ℓ−a)/ℓ≥(w⁡(C)−a)/w⁡(C)(\ell-a)/\ell\geq(w(C)-a)/w(C), from which we see that the image of CC under the homothety with center mm and ratio (w⁡(C)−a)/w⁡(C)(w(C)-a)/w(C) is contained in the image of CC under the homothety with center mm and ratio (ℓ−a)/ℓ(\ell-a)/\ell, which is contained in (C−u)∩(C+u)(C-u)\cap(C+u) as seen above. ∎

Lemma 2.3 might seem to have nothing to do with Theorem 2.2, but we shall rather care about a corollary of this lemma. Note that by successive applications of the preceding lemma on the vectors uju_{j} (remembering that we defined aj=w⁡(Pj)/2a_{j}=w(P_{j})/2 as the length of uju_{j}), we get that the intersection over all 2n2^{n} possible choices of signs ϵj∈{±1}\epsilon_{j}\in\{\pm 1\},

⋂ϵj∈{±1}(C−∑j=1nϵj​uj),\bigcap_{\epsilon_{j}\in\{\pm 1\}}\Big(C-\sum_{j=1}^{n}\epsilon_{j}u_{j}\Big), (2.1)

must contain a homothetic image of CC with a homothety ratio equal to

w⁡(C)−∑i=1nw⁡(Pi)w⁡(C).\frac{w(C)-\sum_{i=1}^{n}w(P_{i})}{w(C)}.

Thus, under the assumption w⁡(P1)+⋯+w⁡(Pn)<w⁡(C)w(P_{1})+\cdots+w(P_{n})<w(C), we can find x0x_{0} in the intersection (2.1) such that xϵ:=x0+∑j=1nϵj​ujx_{\epsilon}:=x_{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\epsilon_{j}u_{j} is in CC for all choices of sign ϵ=(ϵj)j=1n\epsilon=(\epsilon_{j})_{j=1}^{n}. In conjunction with the following lemma, this will lead us to a contradiction.

Lemma 2.4.

For all x0∈ℝdx_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, there is a choice of signs ϵ\epsilon such that xϵ∉Pjx_{\epsilon}\notin P_{j} for j=1,2​…,nj=1,2\ldots,n.

Rather than proving this lemma right away, let us consider another related result that will prove essential in completing this argument and in the following sections of this survey. We will refer to it as Bang’s lemma. The proof follows [14] and [17].

Lemma 2.5 (Bang’s lemma).

Let (ui)i=1n(u_{i})_{i=1}^{n} be unit vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, (mi)i=1n(m_{i})_{i=1}^{n} real numbers, and (wi)i=1n(w_{i})_{i=1}^{n} nonnegative real numbers. Then there is a choice of signs (ϵi)i=1n(\epsilon_{i})_{i=1}^{n} such that the vector x=∑j=1nϵj​wj​ujx=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\epsilon_{j}w_{j}u_{j} satisfies

|⟨x,ui⟩−mi|≥wi|\left\langle x,u_{i}\right\rangle-m_{i}|\geq w_{i}

for all 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n.

Observe that we can reformulate this lemma in the language of linear algebra by introducing a matrix composed of all the possible scalar products between the vectors uiu_{i}, the Gram matrix of (ui)i=1n(u_{i})_{i=1}^{n}. Explicitly, define HH by hi​j=⟨ui,uj⟩h_{ij}=\left\langle u_{i},u_{j}\right\rangle. Then, Lemma 2.5 is equivalent to the existence of a choice of signs (ϵi)i=1n(\epsilon_{i})_{i=1}^{n} such that, for all ii,

|∑j=1nhi​j​ϵj​wj−mi|≥wi.\Bigl|\sum_{j=1}^{n}h_{ij}\epsilon_{j}w_{j}-m_{i}\Bigr|\geq w_{i}.

We refer the reader to Subsection 2.2.2 for a geometric approach to Bang’s lemma and a justification for the choice of the maximizing vector (ϵi)i=1n(\epsilon_{i})_{i=1}^{n}, both of which are due to Bognár.

is maximized. We shall show that this choice of signs satisfies the statement of the lemma. For 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n, let

We could ask that the inequality in Bang’s lemma be strict by using a compactness argument (that is, by slightly modifying the width of our planks if we want to work with open ones). This general argument implies that in plank theorems, we could equivalently work with closed or open planks, and it is explained further in the paragraph following Theorem 3.2.

We are now ready to prove Lemma 2.4.

Proof of Lemma 2.4.

Fix 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n and let pkp_{k} be a point of the middle (or central) hyperplane of PkP_{k}. Note that if zz belongs to one of the boundary hyperplanes of PkP_{k}, then |⟨z−pk,uk⟩|=ak2\absolutevalue{\inner{z-p_k}{u_k}}=a_{k}^{2}, so that PkP_{k} is given explicitly by

{x∈ℝd:|⟨x−pk,uk⟩|≤ak2}.\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\absolutevalue{\inner{x-p_k}{u_k}}\leq a_{k}^{2}\}.

It is now easy to finish the proof of Theorem 2.2. Lemma 2.4 informs us that there is a point which is in CC but in none of the planks that cover CC, a contradiction. Whence it must be that w⁡(P1)+⋯+w⁡(Pn)≥w⁡(C)w(P_{1})+\cdots+w(P_{n})\geq w(C).

2.2.2 A digression on Bognár’s trick

Recall that Lemma 2.4 says that in all the translates of the set

{∑j=1nϵj​uj:ϵj∈{±1}},\Bigl\{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\epsilon_{j}u_{j}:\epsilon_{j}\in\{\pm 1\}\Bigr\},

there exists a point which is not covered by any of the planks that cover the convex body CC, where uju_{j} is the width vector of the jjth plank (as in the proof of Theorem 2.2). Likewise, put simply in terms of plank problems, Bang’s lemma implies that there is a choice of signs (ϵi)i=1n(\epsilon_{i})_{i=1}^{n} such that the point ∑j=1nϵj​wj​uj\sum_{j=1}^{n}\epsilon_{j}w_{j}u_{j} does not belong to any of the open planks

Pi:={x∈ℝd:|⟨x,ui⟩−mi|<wi}P_{i}:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:|\left\langle x,u_{i}\right\rangle-m_{i}|<w_{i}\} (2.2)

that cover CC. The proof given above relies on the optimization of a well-chosen quadratic function on {±1}n\{\pm 1\}^{n}. On the other hand, Bognár’s [35] alternative proof of Theorem 2.2 relies on the observation that it suffices to prove Lemma 2.5 for centered planks, which is sometimes referred to as Bognár’s trick and is still used to simplify the solutions of some discrete geometry problems today (see, for example, the recent papers [52], [53], [59]). Here, by centered planks we mean that their middle (or central) hyperplanes have a common point, or equivalently via a shift, that mi=0m_{i}=0 for all ii. But the proof of Lemma 2.5 in this case is almost immediate, since if for any x0∈ℝdx_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} we pick x′:=x+x0x^{\prime}:=x+x_{0} with maximal norm (where xx is as in the lemma), then

0≤‖x′‖2−‖x′−2​ϵj​wj​uj‖2=4​ϵj​wj​⟨x′,uj⟩−4​wj2,0\leq\|x^{\prime}\|^{2}-\|x^{\prime}-2\epsilon_{j}w_{j}u_{j}\|^{2}=4\epsilon_{j}w_{j}\left\langle x^{\prime},u_{j}\right\rangle-4w_{j}^{2},

which is equivalent to |⟨x′,uj⟩|≥wj|\left\langle x^{\prime},u_{j}\right\rangle|\geq w_{j}. Note that x′−2​ϵj​wj​ujx^{\prime}-2\epsilon_{j}w_{j}u_{j} appeared implicitly in the previous proof of Bang’s lemma when we flipped the sign of the kkth term in the sequence (ϵi)i=1n(\epsilon_{i})_{i=1}^{n}.

To see why it suffices to consider centered planks, we partially follow [5]. Write HiH_{i} for the middle hyperplane of the plank PiP_{i} given by (2.2), think of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} as being embedded in ℝd+1\mathbb{R}^{d+1} as a coordinate subspace

H:={(x,0)∈ℝd+1:x∈ℝd}H:=\{(x,0)\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1}:x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\}

with origin unaltered in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and let ee be a unit vector normal to HH. If ptp_{t} stands for the point t⋅et\cdot e (t>0)(t>0), define hyperplanes HitH_{i}^{t} by pt∈Hitp_{t}\in H_{i}^{t} and Hi⊂HitH_{i}\subset H_{i}^{t}, as well as planks PitP_{i}^{t} with middle hyperplane HitH_{i}^{t} by Pit∩H=PiP_{i}^{t}\cap H=P_{i}. By construction, the PitP_{i}^{t} have a common point ptp_{t}, so we can apply the special case that we have just discussed to deduce that for all t>0t>0, there is a choice of signs (ϵj(t))j=1n(\epsilon_{j}^{(t)})_{j=1}^{n} and a point

y(t)=∑j=1nϵj(t)​wj​ujty^{(t)}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\epsilon_{j}^{(t)}w_{j}u^{t}_{j}

which is in none of the PitP_{i}^{t}, where ujtu_{j}^{t} is the width vector of PjtP_{j}^{t}. Writing y(t)=pt+v(t)y^{(t)}=p_{t}+v^{(t)} for v(t)∈Hv^{(t)}\in H, the sequence (v(t))(v^{(t)}) has a convergent subsequence since its norm is uniformly bounded, say v(tk)→v∈Hv^{(t_{k})}\to v\in H. Because there are only finitely many possible sign vectors, we may pass to a further subsequence where it is constant, say given by (ϵj)j=1n(\epsilon_{j})_{j=1}^{n}. Because ujt→uju_{j}^{t}\to u_{j} as t→∞t\to\infty, the limit point vv has the form

v=∑j=1nϵj​wj​uj.v=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\epsilon_{j}w_{j}u_{j}.

Recall y(t)y^{(t)} is in none of the PitP_{i}^{t}, so projecting onto HH and letting t→∞t\to\infty, we see that vv is not covered by any of the planks PiP_{i}. Thus the centered-limit construction produces the desired sign choice for the original family.

2.2.3 Bang’s generalization of Tarski’s problem

Bang [19] formulated an affine invariant version of Tarski’s plank problem (in the sense that it is invariant under affine transformations of the convex body). If HH is parallel to the boundary hyperplanes of a plank PP, let us call the relative width of PP the ratio w⁡(P)/w⁡(C,H).w(P)/w(C,H).

Conjecture 2.6 (Bang’s conjecture).

If a convex body is covered by a finite number of planks, then the sum of their relative widths is at least 11.

Note that this is strictly stronger than Tarski’s plank problem since w⁡(C,H)≥w⁡(C)w(C,H)\geq w(C). Here are a few more remarks regarding Conjecture 2.6. First, using approximations and affine transformations, Ohmann [75] showed that instead of working with an arbitrary number of planks, it suffices to work with dd planks in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} that are mutually orthogonal and of width 11, for all d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}.

Second, Hunter [58] looked for simple cases of equality in Bang’s conjecture in the plane when the number of planks is given but the convex body can vary. For instance, given a covering of a triangle by three planks, consider the equilateral triangle with sides of unit length that was obtained via affine transformations from the initial triangle. Then it is shown that the sum of the relative widths of the three planks is 11 when and only when the sum of the segments t1+t2+t3t_{1}+t_{2}+t_{3} in Fig. 4 equals 11, where the biggest triangle is the equilateral one prescribed above. The arguments of Hunter also show that Conjecture 2.6 holds for a covering by two planks in the plane, as was also proved in [4, 20, 51, 71]. However, note that the case of a covering by three planks is still open, and it was only recently [3] that Bang’s Conjecture 2.6 was proved for two directions of planks, that is, in the case when the planks can be partitioned into two parallel subfamilies.

Third, Gardner [51] connects Bang’s conjecture with relative width measures for a set of directions, which are Borel probability measures such that the measure of the intersection of CC with each plank orthogonal to one of the directions is equal to the relative width of that plank. He noted that if the convex body CC admits a relative width measure for all directions (in fact, even just for the coordinate directions in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, for all d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}, as in Ohmann’s observation), then Bang’s conjecture holds for CC. He then showed that measures with this property for the coordinate directions always exist for convex bodies in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, yet they generally do not in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}.

Fourth, Alexander [4] observed that this conjecture is equivalent to the following generalization of a theorem of Davenport on intersections of straight lines with unit squares, which is ultimately related to Diophantine approximation in number theory (see Section 6.1 for more details).

Conjecture 2.7 (Reformulation of Conjecture 2.6).

If C⊂ℝdC\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} is a convex body in Euclidean space sliced by n−1n-1 hyperplane cuts, then one of the nn resulting pieces covers a translation of 1n​C\frac{1}{n}C.

This conjecture is known to hold when only successive cuts are used (cutting only one piece into two at each step) [28] and is related to Conway’s fried potato problem, which roughly asks what the radius of the largest ball you can inscribe in at least one of the resulting pieces is. As the authors of [40] put it: “In order to fry it as expeditiously as possible, Conway wishes to slice a given convex potato into nn pieces by n−1n-1 successive plane cuts (just one piece being divided by each cut) so as to minimize the greatest inradius of the pieces.” This problem was solved by A. and K. Bezdek [27, 28] and their proof relies on Bang’s Theorem 2.2.

Conjecture 2.6 is a small modification to Tarski’s conjecture, so one could expect that a similar solution exists. Yet, to this day it remains an important open problem in convex geometry. We shall still see that is has been proven in some specific cases which we will focus on in the upcoming sections.

3 A plank theorem of Ball

3.1 Bang’s conjecture for centrally symmetric convex bodies

In the 1990s, Ball proved Bang’s conjecture in the case where CC is centrally symmetric (for instance, CC symmetric with respect to the origin means that for all x∈Cx\in C, we also have −x∈C-x\in C). In the rest of this section, we shall refer to CC as simply being a symmetric convex body. This supposition on CC allows us to use tools from functional analysis. Indeed, any symmetric convex body can be chosen as the unit ball defining a finite-dimensional normed space, and any such unit ball is a symmetric convex body. To have a definition of a plank in a normed space that is analogous to that of a plank in Euclidean space, we define a plank in a normed space XX by

{x∈X:|ϕ⁡(x)−m|≤w}\left\{x\in X:\absolutevalue{\phi(x)-m}\leq w\right\} (3.1)

for ϕ\phi a continuous linear functional, mm a real number and ww a nonnegative real number. In what follows, we consider unit functionals, so that the relative width of a plank is exactly ww. Here is Ball’s result in this setting [14].

Theorem 3.1.

If the unit ball of a Banach space XX is covered by a set of planks in XX, then the sum of the relative widths of these planks is at least 11.

3.2 Finite-dimensional Banach spaces

The proof ideas presented here mostly follow [14] and [17]. We first consider the case where XX is finite-dimensional, and we shall treat the infinite-dimensional case in Section 3.3. We still suppose that the covering consists of a finite number of planks. We can then reformulate Theorem 3.1 using these hypotheses and (3.1).

Theorem 3.2 (Plank theorem - Finite-dimensional case).

Let XX be a finite-dimensional normed space. Let (ϕi)i=1n(\phi_{i})_{i=1}^{n} be a sequence of unit linear functionals in X∗X^{*}, (mi)i=1n(m_{i})_{i=1}^{n} real numbers and (wi)i=1n(w_{i})_{i=1}^{n} nonnegative real numbers such that ∑i=1nwi=1\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}=1. Then there exists xx in the unit ball of XX such that

|ϕi​(x)−mi|≥wi\absolutevalue{\phi_i(x)-m_i}\geq w_{i}

for all 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n.

If Theorem 3.1 fails, it means there is a family of closed planks covering the unit ball whose total width is <1<1. By replacing them with slightly wider open planks such that the total width is exactly 11, we can apply Theorem 3.2. Hence, the previous theorem can be thought of as a quantitative version of the contrapositive of Theorem 3.1 in the finite-dimensional case. It further justifies that we may choose to work with closed or open planks, as alluded to in the comment following the proof of Lemma 2.5.

3.2.1 Reduction of the plank theorem to a linear algebra problem

Ball’s solution uses a clever mix of tools from functional analysis and linear algebra. The main idea is to obtain a result analogous to Bang’s lemma that holds for matrices that are not necessarily symmetric. We first reduce the problem to purely combinatorial propositions by mimicking some of the ideas that allowed us to express Bang’s lemma in terms of Gram matrices.

Let ϕj\phi_{j} be linear functionals as in the statement of Theorem 3.2. Since XX is finite-dimensional, the unit ball of XX is compact and, in particular, the norm of each ϕj\phi_{j} is attained: we can find xjx_{j} in the unit ball of XX such that ϕj​(xj)=1\phi_{j}(x_{j})=1. Given such xjx_{j}, define the n×nn{\times}n real matrix AA by ai​j=ϕi​(xj)a_{ij}=\phi_{i}(x_{j}). If (λj)j=1n(\lambda_{j})_{j=1}^{n} is a sequence of real numbers such that ∑j=1n|λj|≤1\sum_{j=1}^{n}\absolutevalue{\lambda_j}\leq 1, then x:=∑j=1nλj​xjx:=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\lambda_{j}x_{j} is such that ‖x‖≤1\norm{x}\leq 1 and ϕi​(x)=∑j=1nai​j​λj\phi_{i}(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}\lambda_{j} by linearity. In short, it will suffice to prove the following theorem.

Theorem 3.3.

Let A=(ai​j)1≤i,j≤nA=(a_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq n} be an n×nn{\times}n real matrix with 1′​s1^{\prime}s on the diagonal, (mi)i=1n(m_{i})_{i=1}^{n} real numbers and (wi)i=1n(w_{i})_{i=1}^{n} nonnegative real numbers such that ∑i=1nwi=1\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}=1. Then there exist real numbers (λj)j=1n(\lambda_{j})_{j=1}^{n} such that ∑j=1n|λj|≤1\sum_{j=1}^{n}\absolutevalue{\lambda_j}\leq 1 and

|∑j=1nai​j​λj−mi|≥wi\Bigl|\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}\lambda_{j}-m_{i}\Bigr|\geq w_{i}

for all 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n.

Recall that we interpret wiw_{i} as the width of the iith plank. For arbitrary planks whose total width is <1<1, we may increase the width of each plank so that it becomes rational, yet the total width remains <1<1. Then changing the planks to have rational widths with a common denominator NN, one can split them further into planks of width 1/N1/N. By this density argument, we may suppose that wi=1/nw_{i}=1/n for all ii in what follows. (Here we are implicitly using the fact that the statement of the theorem fails if and only if the convex body is covered by the interiors of a finite number of planks with total width equal to 11.) Also note that if we can show ∑j=1nλj2≤1/n\sum_{j=1}^{n}\lambda_{j}^{2}\leq 1/n, then

(∑j=1n|λj|)2≤n​∑j=1nλj2≤1\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\absolutevalue{\lambda_j}\Bigr)^{2}\leq n\sum_{j=1}^{n}\lambda_{j}^{2}\leq 1

by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.

3.2.2 Proof of Theorem 3.3

The proof of Theorem 3.3 will rely on Bang’s lemma and two new lemmas.

Lemma 3.4.

Let HH be a positive semidefinite symmetric matrix with 1′​s1^{\prime}s on its diagonal. If UU is orthogonal, then

∑i=1n(H​U)i​i2≤n.\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(HU\right)^{2}_{ii}\leq n.

We need to introduce an orthogonal matrix to use Lemma 3.4.

Lemma 3.5.

Let AA be an n×nn{\times}n real matrix with nonzero rows. Then there exist positive real numbers (wi)i=1n(w_{i})_{i=1}^{n} and an orthogonal matrix UU such that the matrix HH defined by

hi​j:=wi​(A​U)i​jh_{ij}:=w_{i}(AU)_{ij}

is positive semidefinite, symmetric, and only has 1′​s1^{\prime}s on its diagonal.

We omit the proofs of these two propositions because they do not rely on ideas that will be used again in the rest of this survey. Lemma 3.4 is a direct consequence of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality stated in terms of the trace of a matrix, and Lemma 3.5 is technical and mostly follows from the polar decomposition of matrices (see [14] for detailed proofs).

By Lemma 3.5, we may take positive real numbers (wj)j=1n(w_{j})_{j=1}^{n} and an orthogonal matrix UU such that H:=(wi​(A​U)i​j)1≤i,j≤nH:=(w_{i}(AU)_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq n} is symmetric, positive semidefinite, and has 1′​s1^{\prime}s on the diagonal. It then follows from Bang’s lemma, in the version formulated in the paragraph following Lemma 2.5, that we can find (ϵj)j=1n(\epsilon_{j})_{j=1}^{n} such that, for all ii,

wi≤|∑j=1nhi​j​ϵj​wj−n​wi​mi|=|wi​∑j=1n(A​U)i​j​ϵj​wj−n​wi​mi|.w_{i}\leq\Bigl|\sum_{j=1}^{n}h_{ij}\epsilon_{j}w_{j}-nw_{i}m_{i}\Bigr|=\Bigl|w_{i}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(AU)_{ij}\epsilon_{j}w_{j}-nw_{i}m_{i}\Bigr|.

Dividing by n⋅win\cdot w_{i}, this is equivalent to

1n≤|∑k=1nai​k​(1n​∑j=1nuk​j​ϵj​wj)−mi|,\frac{1}{n}\leq\Bigl|\sum_{k=1}^{n}a_{ik}\Bigl(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}u_{kj}\epsilon_{j}w_{j}\Bigr)-m_{i}\Bigr|,

which motivates the definition

λk:=1n​∑j=1nuk​j​ϵj​wj.\lambda_{k}:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}u_{kj}\epsilon_{j}w_{j}.

Since UU is orthogonal and ϵj∈{±1}\epsilon_{j}\in\{\pm 1\}, we obtain

∑k=1nλk2=1n2​∑j=1nwj2.\sum_{k=1}^{n}\lambda_{k}^{2}=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j}^{2}.

Also, since H=(wi​(A​U)i​j)H=(w_{i}(AU)_{ij}), we see that

wi​ai​j=(H​U∗)i​j.w_{i}a_{ij}=(HU^{*})_{ij}.

Taking i=ji=j and using ai​i=1a_{ii}=1 yields wi=(H​U∗)i​iw_{i}=(HU^{*})_{ii}. Recall that we want

∑k=1nλk2≤1n,\sum_{k=1}^{n}\lambda_{k}^{2}\leq\frac{1}{n},

so we must show

∑j=1n(H​U∗)j​j2≤n,\sum_{j=1}^{n}(HU^{*})^{2}_{jj}\leq n,

which is precisely the statement of Lemma 3.4 because U∗U^{*} is orthogonal.

3.3 Infinite-dimensional Banach spaces

The goal of this subsection is to prove Theorem 3.1 in the case where XX is an infinite-dimensional Banach space. For reflexive spaces, the result follows readily from the finite-dimensional case (indeed, reflexivity implies that the norm of each functional is attained at some unit vector, as in the beginning of Section 3.2.1). In the general case, the modifications needed in the proof are not obvious, but all the tools we shall need are already available to us. However, since the proof is similar to the finite-dimensional case, we only highlight the differences and refer to [14] for the details. Recall that in the finite case it suffices to obtain a sequence of real numbers (λj)j=1n(\lambda_{j})_{j=1}^{n} that sum to at most 11. However, we obtain something stronger, namely that ∑j=1nλj2≤1/n\sum_{j=1}^{n}\lambda_{j}^{2}\leq 1/n if we suppose that wi=1/nw_{i}=1/n for all ii for simplicity. Running the proof of Theorem 3.3 again with an arbitrary choice of wiw_{i} would instead yield ∑j=1nwj−1​λj2≤∑j=1nwj\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j}^{-1}\lambda_{j}^{2}\leq\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j}. We can thus use the following lemma.

Lemma 3.6.

Let A=(ai​j)1≤i,j≤nA=(a_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq n} be an n×nn{\times}n real matrix with 1′​s1^{\prime}s on the diagonal, (mi)i=1n(m_{i})_{i=1}^{n} real numbers and (wi)i=1n(w_{i})_{i=1}^{n} nonnegative real numbers. Then there exist (λj)j=1n(\lambda_{j})_{j=1}^{n} such that ∑j=1nwj−1​λj2≤∑j=1nwj\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j}^{-1}\lambda_{j}^{2}\leq\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j} and

|∑j=1nai​j​λj−mi|≥wi\Bigl|\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}\lambda_{j}-m_{i}\Bigr|\geq w_{i}

for all 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n.

Also note that it suffices to prove an “infinite” version of Theorem 3.2, where we replace every sequence of nn elements with a sequence indexed by ℕ\mathbb{N}.

Theorem 3.7 (Plank theorem - Infinite-dimensional case).

Let XX be a Banach space. Let (ϕi)i=1∞(\phi_{i})_{i=1}^{\infty} be a sequence of unit functionals in X∗X^{*}, (mi)i=1∞(m_{i})_{i=1}^{\infty} real numbers and (wi)i=1∞(w_{i})_{i=1}^{\infty} nonnegative real numbers such that ∑i=1∞wi<1\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}w_{i}<1. Then there exists xx in the unit ball of XX such that

|ϕi​(x)−mi|>wi\absolutevalue{\phi_i(x)-m_i}>w_{i}

for all ii.

The idea is to choose viv_{i} such that vi>wiv_{i}>w_{i} for all ii, but also such that their sum remains smaller than 11, say ∑i=1∞vi=1−ε<1\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}v_{i}=1-\varepsilon<1. We can find xix_{i} in the unit ball of XX such that ϕi​(xi)=1−ε\phi_{i}(x_{i})=1-\varepsilon, then we apply Lemma 3.6 with a matrix whose i,ji,j entry is ϕi​(xj)/(1−ε)\phi_{i}(x_{j})/(1-\varepsilon). For every nn, we extend the sequences (λj(n))j=1n(\lambda_{j}^{(n)})_{j=1}^{n} that we obtained from Lemma 3.6 to infinite sequences by completing them with zeros. Using a diagonal argument, we obtain a subsequence of (λj(n))n=1∞(\lambda^{(n)}_{j})_{n=1}^{\infty} that converges pointwise for every jj. This allows us to construct the desired point xx.

Note that in the finite case, we used compactness to find points in the unit ball of XX where the norm of the functionals was attained, but now we can only get away with almost attaining their norm.

4 Other types of plank problems and polynomial analogues

We refer to the Theorems 3.2 and 3.7 of Ball as plank theorems without any further distinction, yet they stem from a symmetric plank problem on Banach spaces, and as we shall see in the remaining sections, there are many variations and generalizations of these problems.

4.1 The complex plank problem

Theorem 3.7 is sharp as can be seen by taking X=ℓ1X=\ell_{1} and ϕi\phi_{i} to be the standard basis vectors of ℓ∞\ell_{\infty}, the dual of ℓ1\ell_{1}. However, it is expected that we can improve this result for Hilbert spaces. For instance, Ball proved the following complex Hilbert space analogue of Theorem 3.2 in [16], which turned out to be essential in solving many other problems, as will be discussed in subsequent sections.

Theorem 4.1 (Complex plank theorem).

Let (vj)j=1n(v_{j})_{j=1}^{n} be unit vectors in a complex Hilbert space, and (tj)j=1n(t_{j})_{j=1}^{n} a sequence of nonnegative real numbers such that ∑j=1ntj2=1\sum_{j=1}^{n}t_{j}^{2}=1. Then, there exists a unit vector zz such that

|⟨vj,z⟩|≥tj\absolutevalue{\inner{v_j}{z}}\geq t_{j}

for all 1≤j≤n1\leq j\leq n.

We remark that this plank problem does not involve shifts: it is a complex analogue of the symmetric plank problem for centered planks only (see Section 4.3.1 for a recent, more general complex plank theorem which applies to planks that are not necessarily centrally symmetric). Also, Ball’s proof of the previous theorem has a lot of overlap with the demonstration of Theorem 3.3, so we omit the demonstration here. Let us just mention that the proof reduces to a linear algebra statement as in Section 3.2.1. In particular, this is a reformulation of the case of equal widths tj=1/nt_{j}=1/\sqrt{n}, and the general case follows from technical considerations as outlined in [16].

Proposition 4.2.

Let HH be an n×nn\times{n} complex positive semidefinite hermitian matrix with 1′​s1^{\prime}s on its diagonal. Then there exist complex numbers (wj)j=1n(w_{j})_{j=1}^{n} such that |wj|≤1\absolutevalue{w_j}\leq 1 and

wj​∑khj​k​wk¯=1w_{j}\sum_{k}h_{jk}\overline{w_{k}}=1 (4.1)

for all 1≤j≤n1\leq j\leq n.

To prove this proposition, we can interpret (4.1) as a system of 2​n2n equations by splitting the real and imaginary parts and we can show the existence of a solution using Lagrange multipliers. We then form a new matrix with diagonal entries equal to |wj|2\absolutevalue{w_j}^{2}, and we show that all of these are ≤1\leq 1 using the maximum principle in complex analysis, which finishes the demonstration (see [16] for the details).

4.1.1 Streamlined proof of the complex plank problem

It is important to note that recently, a new and simplified proof of Theorem 4.1 was given by Ortega-Moreno [78] using a versatile polynomial approach, which has proven useful in more recent work on elementary questions regarding zeros of polynomials restricted to the unit sphere. Let us explain his approach by outlining a proof of the complex plank problem for equal widths. The more general case follows from similar ideas.

Theorem 4.3.

Let v1,v2,…,vnv_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{n} be a sequence of unit vectors in ℂd\mathbb{C}^{d}. Then there exists a unit vector u∈ℂdu\in\mathbb{C}^{d} such that

|⟨vk,u⟩|≥1/n|\left\langle v_{k},u\right\rangle|\geq 1/\sqrt{n}

for all 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n.

The statement of Theorem 4.3 holds when uu maximizes ∏i=1n|⟨vi,u⟩|\prod_{i=1}^{n}|\left\langle v_{i},u\right\rangle| among unit vectors. To show this arguing by contradiction, suppose |⟨v1,u⟩|<1/n|\left\langle v_{1},u\right\rangle|<1/\sqrt{n}. Let uz:=z​v1+uu_{z}:=zv_{1}+u whenever zz is such that uz∈Sdu_{z}\in S^{d}. This happens if and only if zz is on the circle CC of radius |⟨v1,u⟩||\left\langle v_{1},u\right\rangle| centered at −⟨u,v1⟩-\left\langle u,v_{1}\right\rangle. Now let pp be the polynomial

p⁡(z)=∏i=2n⟨uz,vk⟩⟨u,vk⟩.p(z)=\prod_{i=2}^{n}\frac{\left\langle u_{z},v_{k}\right\rangle}{\left\langle u,v_{k}\right\rangle}.

We can obtain a contradiction by considering the derivative ∂/∂z¯\partial/\partial\bar{z} of pp at z=0z=0 (where |p⁡(z)||p(z)| reaches its maximum on CC) and applying the maximum modulus principle. We omit the details here because this theorem, albeit simple and straightforward, is dominated by a polynomial analogue statement that we will encounter in Section 4.3 while explaining how this polynomial approach ties in with diverse plank problems.

4.2 The spherical plank problem

This section covers a long-standing conjecture that was recently proven to be true using arguments akin to Bang’s lemma and the plank theorems.

A great circle is the intersection of a sphere in ℝd+1\mathbb{R}^{d+1} and a plane passing through its center, and the spherical distance denotes the shortest distance between two points on the sphere along its surface. These concepts allow us to state a spherical version of the plank problems, where the other definitions are taken mutatis mutandis. Indeed, given a great circle, we say that the analogue of a plank of width ww is a zone of width ww, that is, the set of points that are at spherical distance w/2w/2 or less away from the great circle. Note that zones are not convex in spherical geometry.

4.2.1 Fejes Tóth’s zone conjecture

In 1973, the mathematician L. Fejes Tóth [45] conjectured that if nn zones of equal width ww cover the unit sphere, then ww is at least π/n\pi/n. He was partially motivated by the optimal establishment of nn operating stations on a new planet or the most economical way to explore a planet using nn satellites. He also formulated a more general conjecture where the widths of the zones may vary.

Conjecture 4.4 (Fejes Tóth’s zone conjecture).

The sum of the widths of the zones covering the unit sphere is at least π\pi.

It is straightforward to generalize the previous definitions and Conjecture 4.4 to the unit spheres SdS^{d} embedded in ℝd+1\mathbb{R}^{d+1}, but note that the conclusion of the conjecture would stay the same: it is independent of the ambient dimension. Also, papers by Rosta [83] and Linhart [64] deal with the special cases of coverings by 33 or 44 zones, respectively. It was only in 2017 that Jiang and Polyanskii [59] proved Conjecture 4.4 for the more general unit dd-spheres. Their proof is partly inspired by a paper of Goodman and Goodman [54] on covering of a nonseparable collection of similar copies of a convex body, where the main result is the following circle covering theorem conjectured by Erdős.

Theorem 4.5.

If nn circles with respective radius rir_{i} lie in a plane such that no line divides the circles into two nonempty sets without intersecting any circle, then the nn circles can be covered by one circle of radius ∑i=1nri\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}.

As noted in [59], the spherical analogue of this result should be about spherical caps, the set of points within fixed spherical distance of a given point on the unit dd-sphere, which is the dual of a zone via projective duality (which interchanges a line through the origin with its orthogonal hyperplane through the origin). The cap covering theorem of Polyanskii [81] is both a spherical analogue of the circle covering theorem of Goodman and Goodman and a strengthening of the zone conjecture. We remark that its proof implicitly uses the concept of multi-planks introduced by Balitskiy [13].

Since Jiang and Polyanskii’s resolution of the zone conjecture, streamlined alternative proofs were found and we will present them in Section 4.3, so let us just briefly describe Jiang and Polyanskii’s approach to highlight the similarities it shares with Bang’s solution to Tarski’s plank problem. Suppose that nn zones of width 2​αi2\alpha_{i} cover SdS^{d} embedded in ℝd+1\mathbb{R}^{d+1}, but their total width is less than π\pi. Let HiH_{i} be the middle hyperplane of the iith zone and uiu_{i} be a unit normal vector of HiH_{i}. Consider the set of points of the form

{∑j=1nϵj​uj​sin⁡αj:ϵj∈{±1}},\Bigl\{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\epsilon_{j}u_{j}\sin\alpha_{j}:\epsilon_{j}\in\{\pm 1\}\Bigr\},

and let ww be a point in this set having maximal norm. Then the fact that ‖w‖≥‖w−2​ϵi​ui​sin⁡αi‖\|w\|\geq\|w-2\epsilon_{i}u_{i}\sin\alpha_{i}\| for all ii implies that the distance from ww to HiH_{i} is at least sin⁡αi\sin\alpha_{i}. If ‖w‖<1\|w\|<1, then w/‖w‖w/\|w\| is an element of SdS^{d} that is not covered by the PiP_{i}. We remark that the preceding argument used to find a point that is not covered by the convex hulls of the zones is reminiscent of Bognár’s trick as described in Section 2.2.2. It would also be possible to find it by maximizing a well-chosen quadratic function on {±1}n\{\pm 1\}^{n}, as mentioned in [59], which this time is reminiscent of Bang’s lemma. In the case where ‖w‖≥1\|w\|\geq 1, it can be shown that several zones can be replaced by one zone without increasing the total width, and this argument can be repeated (see [59] for details). We remark that similar ideas are used in [81] to prove a stronger version of the zone conjecture.

4.2.2 A few remarks on Fejes Tóth’s zone conjecture

One may wonder what an optimal plank theorem in real Hilbert spaces would look like. It turns out that a statement as strong as Theorem 4.1 cannot hold, and a rather simple counterexample has been observed by a few people: consider nn equally spaced points on the half-circle, and with their nn antipodal points, call the resulting vectors v1,…,v2​nv_{1},\ldots,v_{2n}. Then, for all unit vectors uu, we can find a kk such that |⟨vk,u⟩|≤sin⁡(π/2​n)\absolutevalue{\inner{v_k}{u}}\leq\sin(\pi/2n), which can be made arbitrarily small.

Still, by giving an explicit description of a zone, we can formulate a spherical plank problem that resembles the previous plank theorems in the case of centered planks. If vv is a unit vector on a given great circle, the associated zone of width ww is

{x∈S1:|⟨v,x⟩|≤sin⁡(w/2)}.\{x\in S^{1}:\absolutevalue{\inner{v}{x}}\leq\sin(w/2)\}.

Then, the following is a reformulation of Conjecture 4.4 in the case of zones of equal width and can be thought of as an optimal plank problem for real Hilbert spaces, in view of the previous example.

Conjecture 4.6 (Reformulation of Fejes Tóth’s zone conjecture for zones of equal width).

Let v1,v2,…,vnv_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{n} be a sequence of unit vectors in a real Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H}. Then there exists a unit vector u∈ℋu\in\mathcal{H} such that

|⟨vk,u⟩|≥sin⁡(π/2​n)\absolutevalue{\inner{v_k}{u}}\geq\sin(\pi/2n)

for all 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n.

An alert reader might have noticed that this is nothing but a spherical variant of Theorem 4.3. We remark that in 2021, a new proof of the Fejes Tóth zone conjecture (for zones of equal width) was given by Ortega-Moreno [77], starting with the previous reformulation. The approach he employs is quite different from the one in Jiang and Polyanskii’s paper and uses the somewhat new concept of inverse eigenvectors in convex geometry, which are used to transform a geometry problem into a study of the behavior of polynomials (they were complex in the complex plank problem, and they are trigonometric in the proof of Conjecture 4.6). We say that a vector xx is an inverse eigenvector of MM if M​x=x−1Mx=x^{-1}, where by definition the iith component of x−1x^{-1} is the inverse of the iith component of xx. These inverse eigenvectors were only formally introduced and defined in [6], but they appear implicitly in the proof of Ball’s plank theorem in the complex case, and in fact you can interpret Proposition 4.2 as saying that every complex positive semidefinite hermitian matrix with 1′​s1^{\prime}s on the diagonal has an inverse eigenvector in the complex ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} unit ball.

Zhao [91] recently simplified the proof of Ortega-Moreno by eliminating the need for the notion of inverse eigenvectors, using instead the polynomial approach that we alluded to in Section 4.1.1. In fact, this is a striking example of how bringing in tools from trigonometry and elementary analysis greatly simplifies a problem that seemed intractable for decades. Let us outline his short and neat argument.

We will show that the statement of Conjecture 4.6 holds when uu is a unit vector that maximizes ∏i=1n|⟨vi,u⟩|\prod_{i=1}^{n}\absolutevalue{\inner{v_i}{u}}. For the sake of contradiction, suppose that |⟨v1,u⟩|<sin⁡(π/2​n)\absolutevalue{\inner{v_1}{u}}<\sin(\pi/2n) and consider the plane spanned by {u,v1}\{u,v_{1}\}. Then we can take a vector w⟂uw\perp u with |w|<1|w|<1 such that, if

uθ:=(cos⁡θ)​u+(sin⁡θ)​w,u_{\theta}:=(\cos\theta)u+(\sin\theta)w,

then uπ/2​n⟂v1u_{\pi/2n}\perp v_{1} (Fig. 6).

Now consider the function

f⁡(θ)=∏i=1n⟨vi,uθ⟩⟨vi,u⟩.f(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\left\langle v_{i},u_{\theta}\right\rangle}{\left\langle v_{i},u\right\rangle}.

We can obtain a contradiction by bounding the number of zeros of f⁡(θ)−cos⁡(n​θ)f(\theta)-\cos(n\theta) in [0,2​π)[0,2\pi). Namely, it can be proven using the intermediate value theorem that f⁡(θ)−cos⁡(n​θ)f(\theta)-\cos(n\theta) has at least 2​n2n distinct zeros in [0,2​π)[0,2\pi), and from considerations on the derivative of ff, that f⁡(θ)−cos⁡(n​θ)f(\theta)-\cos(n\theta) has at most 2​n−22n-2 distinct zeros in [0,2​π)[0,2\pi). We omit the proofs here because they are eclipsed by those of a polynomial zone theorem that we will see in the next section.

4.3 A polynomial approach to plank problems

Here we unite the previous comments on the polynomial approach that was recently used to simplify the demonstration of some plank problems. If we restrict Bang’s Theorem 2.2 to the case of the unit ball, then we know that the sum of the widths of the planks in a covering is at least 22. In particular, if there are nn planks of equal width ww, then w≥2/nw\geq 2/n, which can be interpreted as follows: for any collection of nn hyperplanes in Euclidean space, there exists a point in the unit ball that is at distance at least 1/n1/n from the union of the hyperplanes. Here we note that a hyperplane is the zero set of a degree 11 polynomial, and the union of nn hyperplanes is the zero set of a degree nn polynomial. It is then straightforward to see how the formulations of Theorem 4.3 and Conjecture 4.6 might come to be. In 2022, Glazyrin, Karasev, and Polyanskii [52] devised a polynomial approach to obtain general results on the zeros of polynomials restricted to the unit sphere, which bridged the gap between Tarski’s plank problem and its complex and spherical variants. These ideas can be traced back to the PhD thesis of Ambrus [6] and also to work of Ambrus, Ball, and Erdélyi [8] on the strong polarization problem (see the end of Section 5.1 for more details).

4.3.1 Revisiting the complex and spherical plank problems

Zhao [91] was the first to prove a plank theorem using these ideas by giving a new proof of the zone conjecture for equal widths, and soon after, Ortega-Moreno [78] leveraged the method to simplify the proof of the complex plank problem (see also Sections 4.1.1 and 4.2.2). The following theorems from [52] encapsulate the essence of the arguments of Zhao and Ortega-Moreno by means of results on avoiding zeros of polynomials.

Theorem 4.7.

If a polynomial P∈ℝ⁡[x1,…,xd]P\in\mathbb{R}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}] of degree nn has a nonzero restriction to Sd−1⊂ℝdS^{d-1}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} and attains its maximal absolute value on Sd−1S^{d-1} at a point pp, then pp is at angular distance at least π2​n\frac{\pi}{2n} from the intersection of the zero set of PP with Sd−1S^{d-1}.

Theorem 4.8.

If a homogeneous polynomial P∈ℂ⁡[z1,…,zd]P\in\mathbb{C}[z_{1},\ldots,z_{d}] of degree nn is not identically zero and attains its maximal absolute value on S2​d−1⊂ℂdS^{2d-1}\subset\mathbb{C}^{d} at a point pp, then pp is at angular distance at least arcsin⁡1n\arcsin\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} from the intersection of the zero set of PP with S2​d−1S^{2d-1}.

The homogeneity hypothesis in Theorem 4.8 is essential (see Remark 1.12 in [52]). The authors of [53] found a nonhomogeneous extension of the complex polynomial plank problem which generalizes the complex plank theorem of Ball to planks that are not necessarily centrally symmetric. Since geometrically, a plank in the complex setting is closer to a circular cylinder, here given δi\delta_{i} a positive real number, we refer to the δi\delta_{i}-neighborhood of a complex affine hyperplane in ℂd\mathbb{C}^{d} as a δi\delta_{i}-cylinder.

Theorem 4.9.

If δ1,…,δn>0\delta_{1},\ldots,\delta_{n}>0 satisfy ∑i=1nδi2<R2\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{i}^{2}<R^{2}, then the centered ball of radius RR in ℂd\mathbb{C}^{d} cannot be covered by a union of nn δi\delta_{i}-cylinders.

We shall only prove Theorem 4.7 to showcase the elementary ideas behind these kinds of results, and we refer interested readers to [52] and [53] for the rest. We will also show a stronger result than the zone conjecture: if spherical segments (the portion of a sphere between two parallel hyperplanes, which need not be centrally symmetric) cover Sd−1S^{d-1}, then the sum of their widths is at least π\pi. As noted by the authors, the techniques of Jiang and Polyanskii described in Section 4.2.1 could not be modified to prove this stronger statement. Let us see how the spherical plank problem reduces to this polynomial result. The idea is to approximate spherical segments by unions of thin spherical segments of the same width and apply the polynomial result to the polynomial

H1⋯Hn,H_{1}\cdots H_{n},

where Hi=0H_{i}=0 is the linear equation of the middle hyperplane of the iith segment. The general case is only marginally harder, and in fact the argument is similar to the one that was used to justify picking the same rational width for each plank in Section 3.2.1. Indeed, we obtain a point x∈Sd−1x\in S^{d-1} at spherical distance at least π2​n\frac{\pi}{2n} from every middle hyperplane, and we then proceed by contradiction. First suppose the covering consists of nn spherical segments of equal width 2​δ2\delta. In particular, 2​δ​n<π2\delta n<\pi, or equivalently, π2​n>δ\frac{\pi}{2n}>\delta, so that xx is outside every segment. Second, suppose the nn spherical segments have rational width with common denominator NN. Splitting every spherical segment into several segments of equal width 1/N1/N, this reduces to the previous case. Third, in the general case, suppose once more that the total width is <π<\pi. By density of the rationals in the reals, we may increase the width of each segment so that it becomes rational, yet the total width remains <π<\pi, and the result follows from the previous cases. Now let us turn to the proof of Theorem 4.7 [52].

Proof of Theorem 4.7.

Suppose x0x_{0} is a zero of PP whose angular distance with pp is minimal. By considering the linear span of x0x_{0} and pp, we see that it suffices to prove the result for d=2d=2. We work with the restriction of PP to the unit circle, which allows us to consider PP as a trigonometric polynomial of degree nn by switching to polar coordinates. We can assume PP has maximal absolute value MM at the origin (if not, we simply shift PP). Then our goal is to show that the distance between 00 and the zeros of PP is ≥π2​n\geq\frac{\pi}{2n}. Consider the trigonometric polynomial

Q⁡(x)=P⁡(x)±M​cos⁡(n​x).Q(x)=P(x)\pm M\cos(nx).

We can assume that QQ has zeros of multiplicity 22 at 2​π​k2\pi k, k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z}, by choosing the sign ±\pm appropriately. We will work over a 2​π2\pi-period around the origin, but by this assumption, the argument would work more generally. For m=1,…,2​n−1m=1,\ldots,2n-1,

Q⁡(m​πn)=P⁡(m​πn)±(−1)m​MQ\Bigl(\frac{m\pi}{n}\Bigr)=P\Bigl(\frac{m\pi}{n}\Bigr)\pm(-1)^{m}M

has sign ±(−1)m\pm(-1)^{m} or QQ has a zero of multiplicity 22 at π​m/n\pi m/n. The intermediate value theorem then yields that there are at least 2​n−22n-2 zeros of QQ on (π/n,(2​n−1)​π/n)(\pi/n,(2n-1)\pi/n), counted with multiplicity. Since QQ also has a zero of multiplicity 22 at the origin, QQ has at least 2​n2n zeros per 2​π2\pi-period. If QQ has more zeros (e.g., at −π/n-\pi/n or π/n\pi/n), then QQ is identically zero and the conclusion holds; otherwise, QQ has no zeros on [−π/n,π/n][-\pi/n,\pi/n], except at 00. In this case, it must be strictly positive (respectively strictly negative) on (0,π/n)(0,\pi/n) (respectively (−π/n,0)(-\pi/n,0)); but if P⁡(x0)=0P(x_{0})=0 for some x0x_{0} in (−π2​n,π2​n)(-\frac{\pi}{2n},\frac{\pi}{2n}), then cos⁡(n​x0)>0\cos(nx_0)>0 and so Q⁡(x0)Q(x_{0}) is of opposite sign to what was derived above, a contradiction. Hence there are no zeros of PP in (−π2​n,π2​n)(-\frac{\pi}{2n},\frac{\pi}{2n}), which yields the desired result. Note that in the above, the bound is sharp precisely when Q=0Q=0. ∎

4.3.2 More remarks on the polynomial analogues of plank problems

It is worth noting that this polynomial approach works on the complex and spherical plank problems because they do not involve shifts, they concern centered planks. One could say that they are really polarization problems (as in Section 5.1). It follows that these polynomial arguments are unlikely to yield a streamlined demonstration of Ball’s Theorem 3.2. Finding a simplification of the proof of the original plank theorem of Ball is thus an intriguing problem. Nonetheless, a tight polynomial analogue of Bang’s Theorem 2.2 for a ball can be obtained with a little more work using these ideas [52].

Theorem 4.10.

For every n≥1n\geq 1, there exists a sequence of analytic functions Gn:ℝ→ℝG_{n}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} such that for every nonzero polynomial P∈ℝ⁡[x1,…,xd]P\in\mathbb{R}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}] of degree nn, the point in the unit ball BdB^{d} of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} where P⁡(x)​Gn​(|x|)P(x)G_{n}(|x|) attains its maximum on BdB^{d} is at distance at least 1/n1/n from the zero set of PP.

The functions GnG_{n} are explicitly given by gn​(n​π​x/2)g_{n}(n\pi x/2), where

gn​(x):={∏i=n2+1∞(1−(2​x(2​i−1)​π)2)if n is even,∏i=n+12∞(1−(xi​π)2)if n is odd,g_{n}(x):=\begin{cases}\prod_{i=\frac{n}{2}+1}^{\infty}\Bigl(1-\Bigl(\frac{2x}{(2i-1)\pi}\Bigr)^{2}\Bigr)&if $n$ is even,\\ \prod_{i=\frac{n+1}{2}}^{\infty}\Bigl(1-\Bigl(\frac{x}{i\pi}\Bigr)^{2}\Bigr)&if $n$ is odd,\end{cases}

which is to be compared with the infinite product representation of the trigonometric functions sin⁡(x)\sin(x) and cos⁡(x)\cos(x).

The proof of Theorem 4.10 is more intricate than the one from Section 4.3.1, yet it reduces to a spherical polynomial result (which says slightly more than Theorem 4.7) by approximating the ball by a cap of a sphere of large radius, then chopping the area between this cap and the opposite one in spherical segments of equal widths. The spherical case needs to be carefully applied to a polynomial of the form P⋅GRP\cdot G_{R}, where RR corresponds to the radius of the sphere and is chosen such that it is almost impossible to have a maximum of |P⋅GR||P\cdot G_{R}| on the sphere outside the cap. Then one needs to take the limit as RR goes to infinity, being careful about uniform convergence on compact subsets. We refer the reader to [52] for the details.

Let us end this section with the following enticing conjecture on covering a sphere by planks instead of zones.

Conjecture 4.11.

If Sd−1S^{d-1}, d≥4d\geq 4, is covered by planks P1,…,PnP_{1},\ldots,P_{n}, then

w⁡(P1)+⋯+w⁡(Pn)≥2.w(P_{1})+\cdots+w(P_{n})\geq 2.

It is unlikely that the previous polynomial approach will bear fruit with regards to this conjecture, since the arguments first reduced the problem to the d=2d=2 case, which is false here (in fact, it is readily seen that a covering of S1S^{1} by planks of arbitrarily small widths is possible). But it is known to hold for d=3d=3 [70] and for d=4d=4 when there are at most three planks [52].

4.4 Strengthening the plank theorems and plank problems in other settings

Another natural problem to consider in discrete geometry is that of covering by arbitrary convex bodies, which can serve as a strengthening of the questions on covering by planks. The inradius of CC is the radius of the largest ball contained in CC and is denoted by r⁡(C)r(C). It has been shown [26] that if the closed unit disk is partitioned by 22-dimensional convex bodies C1,…,CnC_{1},\ldots,C_{n} (sometimes called convex cells), then

∑i=1nr⁡(Ci)≥1.\sum_{i=1}^{n}r(C_{i})\geq 1. (4.2)

Note that this result is stronger than Tarski’s plank problem for the unit disk in the sense that even if you partition the disk into mm cells CiC_{i} and for each cell pick the narrowest plank that contains it, the sum of those minimal widths is still at least 22. Indeed, each such plank will have width greater than or equal to the diameter of the incircle of the cell, namely 2​r​(Ci)2r(C_{i}), so that ∑i=1nwi≥∑i=1m2​r​(Ci)≥2\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}\geq\sum_{i=1}^{m}2r(C_{i})\geq 2. The proof of (4.2) is also reminiscent of the arguments of Tarski that were outlined in Section 2.1.1. If we consider coverings of the unit ball of Banach spaces by convex bodies, then these subadditivity of the inradii questions improve the plank theorems. For example, while the following result remains open for general Banach spaces, it has been shown by Kadets [60] (and much earlier by Ohmann [76] in the planar case) that if CC is a convex body in a Hilbert space which is covered by convex bodies C1,C2,…C_{1},C_{2},\ldots, then

∑i=1∞r⁡(Ci∩C)≥r⁡(C).\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}r(C_{i}\cap C)\geq r(C). (4.3)

It is sufficient to prove the result when CC is the unit ball of the Hilbert space HH, so we immediately see how it relates to Ball’s symmetric plank theorem. It also relies primarily on the following generalization of Bang’s lemma (which follows from an amalgamation of the results found in [60]).

Proposition 4.12.

If U1,…,UnU_{1},\ldots,U_{n} are finite sets of unit vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} such that 00 is in the convex hull of each UiU_{i}, (wi)i=1n(w_{i})_{i=1}^{n} are nonnegative real numbers and (vi)i=1n(v_{i})_{i=1}^{n} are vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, then there exists ui∈Uiu_{i}\in U_{i} (i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n) so that u=∑i=1nwi​uiu=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}u_{i} satisfies

⟨u−vi,ui⟩≥wi\left\langle u-v_{i},u_{i}\right\rangle\geq w_{i}

for all 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n.

To see how it generalizes Lemma 2.5, if u1,…,unu_{1},\ldots,u_{n} are unit vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and mim_{i} are real numbers, simply take Ui={ui,−ui}U_{i}=\{u_{i},-u_{i}\} and pick viv_{i} so that ⟨vi,ui⟩=mi\left\langle v_{i},u_{i}\right\rangle=m_{i}.

Bang’s lemma and results like (4.2) and (4.3) have been explored and generalized in other ways. For instance, there have been recent extensions to the notion of generalized nonconvex multi-planks [13] (which also apply Bognár’s trick) and to contact pairs in the spirit of the Colorful Carathéodory Theorem [7]. It is also known that an analogue of (4.3) holds for coverings of large balls in spherical space [33], and that an analogue of (4.2) holds for the inradius relative to a convex body C⊂ℝdC\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} [2], which for a convex set D⊂ℝdD\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} is defined by

rC​(D):=sup{λ≥0:∃x∈ℝd​ such that ​λ​C+x⊂D}r_{C}(D):=\sup\{\lambda\geq 0:\>\exists\>x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\text{ such that }\lambda C+x\subset D\}

with rC​(∅)=−∞r_{C}(\emptyset)=-\infty, once we replace arbitrary coverings by certain convex partitions. Here a partition is a covering by a family of closed convex sets with disjoint interiors. Even for ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, there exist coverings that do not contain partitions, for instance planks going through the center of a disk such that their intersection with the boundary of the disk forms two disjoint arcs and all of these arcs partition the boundary, thus forming a “sunflower”. The authors of [2] prove that the analogue of Kadets’ theorem in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} holds for any partition.

Theorem 4.13.

Let C⊂ℝ2C\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be a convex body with convex partition C1∪⋯Cn=CC_{1}\cup\cdots C_{n}=C. Then

∑i=1nrC​(Ci)≥1.\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{C}(C_{i})\geq 1.

However, in higher dimensions, they need to restrict to convex partitions induced by inductive partitions of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} (see [2]). The key idea is that any convex partition C1∪⋯∪Cn=C⊂ℝ2C_{1}\cup\cdots\cup C_{n}=C\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} can be extended to a partition V1∪⋯∪VnV_{1}\cup\cdots\cup V_{n} of all of ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, so in this case the inductive approach always works: we consider translations of the ViV_{i}’s by a vector yy which we can pick such that one of the (Vi+y)∩C(V_{i}+y)\cap C disappears, so we can remove it from the partition, then repeat the process on the partition into fewer parts. Also note that analogues for infinite-dimensional Banach spaces can be obtained via standard approximation arguments, and that while a version of Kadets’ theorem holds in the context of spherical geometry, it does not work for hyperbolic space.

Let us also mention that coverings by specific convex bodies have been investigated. For instance, a question on covering by cylinders was actually introduced by Bang [19]. He noted that while Theorem 2.2 means that the least 11-dimensional projection of a convex body is not greater than the sum of the 11-dimensional projections of its parts, the analogous statement for 22-dimensional projections does not hold. K. Bezdek and Litvak [32] were then motivated to study the following question.

Question 4.14.

Is the sum of the base areas of finitely many cylinders covering a 33-dimensional convex body at least half of the minimum area of a 22-dimensional projection of the body?

If true, this would be sharp as implied by an example of Bang [19]. While the answer to Question 4.14 is still unknown, the authors of [32] were able to show that the sum in question is at least one-third of the minimum area of a 22-dimensional projection of the convex body covered by cylinders. On a related note, the following appealing special case of a conjecture of A. Bezdek [25] on the covering of annuli by planks remains open.

Conjecture 4.15.

If a sufficiently small concentric circular hole is removed from a unit disk and the resulting annulus is covered by planks, then the total width of the covering is at least 11.

In other words, the planks that cover the annulus can be rearranged to cover the entire unit disk. One can see that the analogous statement for convex domains in the plane does not hold in general (it fails for an equilateral triangle, for example), although it was stated in this form at first as a variant of Bang’s problem. In [89], the polygons for which it holds were characterized, and recent work [10] extended this to convex bodies in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} and ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} having a minimal width direction in which it is “spiky” (as defined in [89] and [10]).

4.4.1 Completing the picture in settings other than the Euclidean space

We have seen examples of plank theorems for general Banach and Hilbert spaces, but we can formulate plank problems in other settings or give more precise theorem statements in some cases.

The reader is advised to compare the following Lp​(μ)L_{p}(\mu) plank theorem from [82] with Theorem 4.1, where Lp​(μ)L_{p}(\mu) stands for the set of measurable functions ff such that ∫|f|p​𝑑μ<∞\int|f|^{p}\,d\mu<\infty.

Theorem 4.16.

If f1,…,fn∈Lp​(μ)∗f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\in L_{p}(\mu)^{*} are unit functionals, then there is a point xx in the unit ball of Lp​(μ)L_{p}(\mu) such that for 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n,

|fk​(x)|≥{n−1/p,1≤p≤2,n−1/q,2≤p≤∞,|f_{k}(x)|\geq\begin{cases}n^{-1/p},&1\leq p\leq 2,\\ n^{-1/q},&2\leq p\leq\infty,\end{cases}

where qq is the conjugate exponent of pp, that is, 1/p+1/q=11/p+1/q=1.

Observe that for p=1p=1 and p=∞p=\infty, we obtain |fk​(x)|≥1/n|f_{k}(x)|\geq 1/n, which was already known from Ball’s plank theorems. Let us look at the simple proof of Theorem 4.16 from [82] to realize that this is, indeed, just an extension of the complex plank theorem.

Proof.

We will need one fact about the Banach–Mazur distance between normed spaces which are isomorphic as vector spaces,

d(X,Y)=inf{‖T‖∥T−1∥∣T:X→Y is an isomorphism},d(X,Y)=\inf\{\norm{T}\|{T^{-1}}\|\mid T:X\to Y\text{ is an isomorphism}\},

which is that if EE is a dd-dimensional subspace of Lp​(μ)L_{p}(\mu), then d⁡(E,ℓ2d)≤d|1/2−1/p|d(E,\ell_{2}^{d})\leq d^{|1/2-1/p|} (see [63] for the proof).

As just observed, the cases p=1p=1 and p=∞p=\infty are dealt with already, and when 1<p<∞1<p<\infty, Lp​(μ)L_{p}(\mu) is reflexive so we can find xkx_{k} in the unit ball of Lp​(μ)L_{p}(\mu) for which |fk​(xk)|=‖fk‖=1|f_{k}(x_{k})|=\|f_{k}\|=1 for all 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n. Now consider E:=span​{x1,…,xn}E:=\text{span}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}, which has dimension d≤nd\leq n. Then gk:=fk|E\left.g_{k}:=f_{k}\right|_{E} is such that ‖gk‖=1\|g_{k}\|=1 and using our fact on the Banach–Mazur distance, we can find an isomorphism TT from ℓ2d\ell_{2}^{d} to EE such that ‖T‖=1\|T\|=1 and ‖T−1‖≤d|1/2−1/p|\|T^{-1}\|\leq d^{|1/2-1/p|}.

We are now in a position to apply Theorem 4.1, which gives us a unit x0∈ℓ2dx_{0}\in\ell_{2}^{d} for which |(gk∘T)​(x0)|≥‖gk∘T‖/n|(g_{k}\circ T)(x_{0})|\geq\|g_{k}\circ T\|/\sqrt{n}. Let x:=T​x0x:=Tx_{0}. Then ‖x‖≤‖T‖​‖x0‖=1\|x\|\leq\|T\|\|x_{0}\|=1 and

|fk​(x)|=|gk​(x)|=|gk​(T​x0)|≥‖gk∘T‖n≥‖gk‖/‖T−1‖n=1n1/2​‖T−1‖≥1n1/2​d|12−1p|.|f_{k}(x)|=|g_{k}(x)|=|g_{k}(Tx_{0})|\geq\frac{\|g_{k}\circ T\|}{\sqrt{n}}\geq\frac{\|g_{k}\|/\|T^{-1}\|}{\sqrt{n}}=\frac{1}{n^{1/2}\|T^{-1}\|}\geq\frac{1}{n^{1/2}d^{|\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{p}|}}.

This proves the claim. ∎

Now let us consider a discrete plank problem. A lattice of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} is an additive subgroup of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} that is isomorphic to ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d} and that spans ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Equivalently, it corresponds to the set of all linear combinations with integer coefficients of the elements of a basis of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. We say that a convex set of lattice points is the intersection of a convex body with a lattice. Extending plank problems to this discrete setting, it is natural to study coverings of these convex sets by specific subspaces like hyperplanes. A long-standing and shockingly simple to state conjecture in the area, due to Corzatt [39], states that if a convex set of lattice points can be covered by nn lines, then these lines can be taken to have at most four different slopes (see Fig. 7 for an example).

This conjecture is reminiscent of the disk case (n=2n=2) of Tarski’s problem, which was proven first, but can be extended to higher dimensions as in Tarski’s plank problem. Recall from the Introduction that in the covering of convex bodies in the plane, a parallel covering is optimal. You can think of this as saying that we only require one parallel class to cover the convex body. Then one can wonder more generally about the previous conjecture whether for all dimension dd and for all sets of convex lattice points in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, their coverings can be taken to have at most a constant (depending on dd) number of parallel classes. A close problem of Brass [37] asks to find the smallest constant c⁡(d)c(d) such that if a convex set of lattice points in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} is covered by nn hyperplanes, then it can also be covered by c⁡(d)⋅nc(d)\cdot n parallel hyperplanes.

Related to this is the notion of lattice width, as investigated first by K. Bezdek and Hausel [31]. The lattice width of a convex body in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with respect to the integer lattice ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d} is defined as

wℤd​(C)=miny∈ℤd∖{0}⁡{maxx∈C⁡⟨x,y⟩−minx∈C⁡⟨x,y⟩}.w_{\mathbb{Z}^{d}}(C)=\min_{y\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}\setminus\{0\}}\Bigl\{\max_{x\in C}\left\langle x,y\right\rangle-\min_{x\in C}\left\langle x,y\right\rangle\Bigr\}.

This number is used to give a lower bound on the number of hyperplanes needed to cover C∩ℤdC\cap\mathbb{Z}^{d}. It is conjectured that if nn hyperplanes are used, then n≥wℤd​(C)−dn\geq w_{\mathbb{Z}^{d}}(C)-d. If true, this would be best possible [31]. It is known that the following weaker result holds [86].

Theorem 4.17.

If CC is a convex body in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} covered by nn hyperplanes, then

n≥c⋅wℤd​(C)d−d,n\geq c\cdot\frac{w_{\mathbb{Z}^{d}}(C)}{d}-d,

where c>0c>0 is an absolute constant.

Note that this result implies that the constant c⁡(d)c(d) alluded to in the aforementioned problem of Brass is at most c⋅d2c\cdot d^{2}.

Furthermore, Ball’s plank theorem has been used to improve Theorem 4.17 for centrally symmetric convex bodies whose lattice width is at most quadratic in dimension [32]. In particular, the argument relies on Corollary 6.3 that will be presented in Section 6.1. The lower bound obtained is

n≥c⋅wℤd​(C)d​ln⁡(d+1).n\geq c\cdot\frac{w_{\mathbb{Z}^{d}}(C)}{d\ln(d+1)}.

A similar problem asks to determine the minimal number of hyperplanes needed to cover the vertices of the hypercube {±1}n\{\pm 1\}^{n}. Clearly, two hyperplanes suffice (e.g., given by x1=1x_{1}=1 and x1=−1x_{1}=-1), but this is only a “11-dimensional” covering, and so we would like to ask that each variable x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n} is used in the equations defining the hyperplanes covering the vertices. But this problem is still not interesting, because one could add a redundant equation, e.g., x1+⋯+xn=0x_{1}+\cdots+x_{n}=0, to obtain a covering with 33 hyperplanes. But this new hyperplane is not really needed, so it is natural to also ask that none of the hyperplanes in the covering are redundant. This leads to the notion of an essential cover of the nn-dimensional hypercube, introduced by Linial and Radhakrishnan [65]. If e⁡(n)e(n) stands for the smallest size of an essential cover of {±1}n\{\pm 1\}^{n}, then they showed

4​n+1+12≤e⁡(n)≤⌈n2⌉+1.\frac{\sqrt{4n+1}+1}{2}\leq e(n)\leq\Big\lceil\frac{n}{2}\Big\rceil+1.

The upper bound is still the best known to date, but the lower bound has been improved in a series of works by different authors which all use Bang’s lemma in their proof. It was shown that the lower bound can be taken to be C1⋅n0.52C_{1}\cdot n^{0.52} in [90], C2⋅n5/9/(log⁡n)4/9C_{2}\cdot n^{5/9}/(\log n)^{4/9} in [11], and C3⋅n2/3​(log⁡n)2/3C_{3}\cdot n^{2/3}(\log n)^{2/3} in [84], for some positive constants CiC_{i} and all nn large enough.

Of particular interest to some authors are inverse plank problems, that is, how to guarantee that certain systems of planks (or more generally convex bodies) can cover a given convex set (see [56], [62], and [67]). We often talk of permitting a translative covering of a convex set. Some authors have also recently used techniques of symplectic geometry to study plank problems. In particular, they propose symplectic capacities (invariants of symplectic manifolds that have already proven to be useful in problems at the intersection of convex and symplectic geometry) as a vehicle to reformulate plank problems and to pose a question stronger than the known plank problems. For the specific definitions and statements given by the authors, see the paper [3] and the references therein.

It is important to note that we have not covered all of the types of plank problems that have been investigated in the literature. However, from our above exposition we can see that the proofs of the plank problems can be categorized based on the methods used. We distinguish a few main approaches as follows. A volumetric approach such as the one used by Tarski (and Moese) in the proof of Tarski’s plank problem for a disk in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} and a sphere in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}; one based on optimization arguments as in Bang’s lemma and its generalizations; one using matrix methods as in Ball’s proof of the symmetric plank theorem and its complex counterpart; a polynomial approach to plank problems as in Section 4.3; and other ad hoc approaches, for example the deformation argument that was used to prove an analogue of Kadets’ theorem for certain convex partitions (see the discussion surrounding Theorem 4.13). Finally, consult [29, 30] or [37, Section 3.4] to find more open problems and conjectures that are related to plank problems.

5 Applications in analysis

We continue to survey applications of plank theorems in different fields by looking into various problems coming from analysis.

5.1 Polarization problems and linear polarization constants

The real polarization problem states that for any unit vectors u1,…,un∈ℝdu_{1},\ldots,u_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, we can find a unit vector v∈ℝdv\in\mathbb{R}^{d} such that

∏k=1n|⟨uk,v⟩|≥n−n/2,\prod_{k=1}^{n}|\left\langle u_{k},v\right\rangle|\geq n^{-n/2}, (5.1)

and that equality is attained only if the uku_{k} form an orthonormal system in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} (see [6], [68]). Similar problems arise from the concept of linear polarization constants. Formally, for XX a Banach space, define the nnth linear polarization constant of XX as

cn​(X)\displaystyle c_{n}(X) :=inf{M>0:‖ϕ1‖⋯‖ϕn‖≤M‖ϕ1⋯ϕn‖ for all ϕ1,…,ϕn∈X∗}\displaystyle:=\inf\{M>0:\norm{\phi_1}\cdots\norm{\phi_n}\leq M\norm{\phi_1\cdots\phi_n}\text{ for all }\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{n}\in X^{*}\}
=1/infϕ1,…,ϕn∈SX∗sup‖x‖=1|ϕ1(x)⋯ϕn(x)|,\displaystyle=1/\inf_{\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{n}\in S_{X^{*}}}\sup_{\|x\|=1}|\phi_{1}(x)\cdots\phi_{n}(x)|, (5.2)

where SX∗S_{X^{*}} is the unit sphere of X∗X^{*}, the dual space of XX. Note that cn​(X)c_{n}(X) is an isometric invariant of XX. Here is one example of the nnth linear polarization constant: it follows from Theorem 4.16 that

cn​(Lp​(μ))≤{nn/p,1≤p≤2,nn/q,2≤p≤∞.c_{n}(L_{p}(\mu))\leq\begin{cases}n^{n/p},&1\leq p\leq 2,\\ n^{n/q},&2\leq p\leq\infty.\end{cases}

Furthermore, if dimLp​(μ)≥n\dim L_{p}(\mu)\geq n, then this result is sharp when 1≤p≤21\leq p\leq 2 [82].

Several authors have been interested in the polarization constant of XX, namely

c⁡(X):=lim supn→∞cn​(X)1/n.c(X):=\limsup_{n\to\infty}c_{n}(X)^{1/n}.

As it was shown in [82], the limit always exists and so we may replace lim supn→∞\limsup_{n\to\infty} by limn→∞\lim_{n\to\infty} in the definition of c⁡(X)c(X). It is natural to wonder what we can infer on c⁡(X)c(X) depending on XX. At first glance, it is hard to say much more than c⁡(X)≥1c(X)\geq 1, so perhaps it is often the case that c⁡(X)=∞c(X)=\infty. Fortunately, it has been proven that c⁡(X)=∞c(X)=\infty if and only if dimX=∞X=\infty [82]. Most of the study of the polarization constant of XX relies on bounds for cn​(X)c_{n}(X). For instance, it has been shown that in complex Banach spaces, cn​(X)≤nnc_{n}(X)\leq n^{n}, which is best possible [24]. Indeed, the coordinate functionals

ϕi:ℓ1n​(ℂ)\displaystyle\phi_{i}\colon\ell_{1}^{n}(\mathbb{C}) →ℂ\displaystyle\to\mathbb{C}
(z1,…,zn)\displaystyle(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}) ↦zi\displaystyle\mapsto z_{i}

give

‖ϕ1‖⋯‖ϕn‖=nn‖ϕ1⋯ϕn‖.\norm{\phi_1}\cdots\norm{\phi_n}=n^{n}\norm{\phi_1\cdots\phi_n}.

Surprisingly, it was proven a few years later that the same upper bound cn​(X)≤nnc_{n}(X)\leq n^{n} holds true in real Banach spaces and is also best possible. It simply follows from Ball’s plank theorem 3.2 upon picking mi=0m_{i}=0 and wi=1/nw_{i}=1/n in the statement of the theorem, as first observed in [82].

While it is inherently hard to calculate the nnth polarization constant of specific Banach spaces, the study of cn​(ℓ2n​(𝕂))c_{n}(\ell_{2}^{n}(\mathbb{K})), where 𝕂=ℝ\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{R} or ℂ\mathbb{C}, is of utmost importance, since from [82] we know that

cn​(ℓ2n​(𝕂))≤cn​(X)≤nn/2​cn​(ℓ2n​(𝕂))c_{n}(\ell_{2}^{n}(\mathbb{K}))\leq c_{n}(X)\leq n^{n/2}c_{n}(\ell_{2}^{n}(\mathbb{K})) (5.3)

for all infinite-dimensional Banach spaces XX. You can think of this lower bound as saying that Hilbert spaces have the smallest nnth polarization constants among infinite-dimensional Banach spaces. The proof uses the concept of the Banach–Mazur distance between two isomorphic Banach spaces that we alluded to in Section 4.4.1.

The next step is to inquire what happens for Hilbert spaces, where we modify the definition of the polarization constant according to the Riesz representation theorem. We may also see that

cn(X)=sup{cn(Y):Y is a closed subspace of X,dimY≤n}c_{n}(X)=\sup\{c_{n}(Y):Y\text{ is a closed subspace of }X,\dim Y\leq n\}

when XX is a Hilbert space. Observe that from Ball’s complex plank theorem, there exists a unit vector zz such that |⟨vj,z⟩|≥1/n|\left\langle v_{j},z\right\rangle|\geq 1/\sqrt{n} for unit vectors v1,…,vnv_{1},\ldots,v_{n} and 1≤j≤n1\leq j\leq n, whence

|⟨v1,z⟩|⋯|⟨vn,z⟩|≥n−n/2.|\left\langle v_{1},z\right\rangle|\cdots|\left\langle v_{n},z\right\rangle|\geq n^{-n/2}. (5.4)

This is the complex version of the polarization problem presented at the beginning of the section, and comparing with (5.2), we see that it implies cn​(H)≤nn/2c_{n}(H)\leq n^{n/2} for HH a complex Hilbert space.
