This was proven a few years prior to Ball’s result by Arias-de-Reyna [12] using results on permanents and Gaussian random variables, and it was also shown that cn​(ℓ2n​(ℂ))=nn/2c_{n}(\ell_{2}^{n}(\mathbb{C}))=n^{n/2}, so it follows from (5.3) that cn​(H)=nn/2c_{n}(H)=n^{n/2} when dimH≥n\dim H\geq n. Note that by the nonhomogeneous polynomial complex plank theorem seen in Section 4.3.1, we have a nonhomogeneous extension of (5.4) (this was stated in [53] with a typo in the result): for unit vectors v1,…,vnv_{1},\ldots,v_{n} and all vectors y1,…,yny_{1},\ldots,y_{n}, there exists a unit vector zz such that

|⟨v1,z−y1⟩|⋯|⟨vn,z−yn⟩|≥n−n/2.|\left\langle v_{1},z-y_{1}\right\rangle|\cdots|\left\langle v_{n},z-y_{n}\right\rangle|\geq n^{-n/2}.

Analogously to the Banach space case, it is conjectured that the same constant works for real Hilbert spaces, which was proven for n≤5n\leq 5 in [79] and recently for n≤14n\leq 14 in [80]. Similarly, it is also expected that cn​(ℓ2n​(ℝ))=nn/2c_{n}(\ell_{2}^{n}(\mathbb{R}))=n^{n/2}. Note that the real polarization problem presented at the beginning of this section would imply this conjecture. We cannot expect to find a proof using known plank theorems, for even though Ball’s complex plank theorem is sharp in complex Hilbert spaces, it does not hold for real Hilbert spaces (see Section 4.2.2). Nevertheless, many authors have provided upper bounds for the polarization constant of real Hilbert spaces. A simple argument follows from the result on complex Hilbert spaces along with the complexification of a real Hilbert space HH, yielding cn​(H)≤2n/2−1​nn/2c_{n}(H)\leq 2^{n/2-1}n^{n/2}, and the best result is from [49] and gives

cn​(H)<(3​3e​n)n/2<(1.912​n)n/2.c_{n}(H)<\Bigl(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{e}n\Bigr)^{n/2}<(1.912n)^{n/2}.

Another polarization problem has been investigated, deemed more interesting from a geometric point of view. It states that given unit vectors u1,…,unu_{1},\ldots,u_{n} in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, there exists a unit vector v∈ℝdv\in\mathbb{R}^{d} such that

∑i=1n1⟨ui,v⟩2≤n2.\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\left\langle u_{i},v\right\rangle^{2}}\leq n^{2}. (5.5)

Note that this is stronger than the real polarization problem presented earlier because the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality yields

∏i=1n(1⟨ui,v⟩2)1/n≤1n​∑i=1n1⟨ui,v⟩2≤n,\prod_{i=1}^{n}\Bigl(\frac{1}{\left\langle u_{i},v\right\rangle^{2}}\Bigr)^{1/n}\leq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\left\langle u_{i},v\right\rangle^{2}}\leq n,

which is equivalent to (5.1). It was shown in [8] that if z1,…,zn∈S1z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}\in S^{1}, then there exists z∈S1z\in S^{1} such that

∑k=1n1|zk−z|2≤n24,\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{|z_{k}-z|^{2}}\leq\frac{n^{2}}{4},

which settled the d=2d=2 case of the previous polarization problem. Indeed, thinking of this case as being formulated on the complex unit circle, we are given u1,…,un∈S1u_{1},\ldots,u_{n}\in S^{1}, say uk=(cos⁡(tk/2),sin⁡(tk/2)){u_{k}=(\cos(t_k/2),\sin(t_k/2))}, and we are looking for v∈S1v\in S^{1} such that (5.5) holds. Writing

v=(cos⁡t−π2,sin⁡t−π2),v=\big(\cos\frac{t-\pi}{2},\sin\frac{t-\pi}{2}\big),

z=ei​tz=e^{it}, and zk=ei​tkz_{k}=e^{it_{k}}, then ⟨uk,v⟩\left\langle u_{k},v\right\rangle reduces to |z−zk|/2|z-z_{k}|/2 after using trigonometric identities. These ideas have been generalized and formal definitions as well as several related results on polarization can be found in [36, Chapter 14].

We also remark that both of the polarization problems presented in this section can be reformulated in terms of inverse eigenvectors, which were introduced briefly in Section 4.2.2, and this connects them more deeply with the complex plank problem. The ideas that appear in the proofs of polarization problems are also connected with the polynomial approach presented in Section 4.3, as already mentioned there.

5.2 Applications in functional analysis

Let us first mention that plank theorems can be interpreted as a strengthening or extensions of well-known theorems. For example, Conjecture 2.7 is a reformulation of Bang’s conjecture and can be interpreted as a geometric version of the pigeonhole principle. Thus, Theorem 3.1 is in some sense a geometric pigeonhole principle for convex symmetric bodies. Many other examples come from functional analysis.

5.2.1 Classical results in functional analysis

Plank theorems have connections with fundamental theorems in functional analysis. Recall that the Hahn–Banach theorem roughly says that linear functionals on a linear subspace can be extended to the whole normed space while preserving the norm. Using the weak-∗ topology of X∗X^{*} (the smallest topology such that every element of XX is continuous with respect to that topology), we can “inverse” Theorem 3.7 to obtain a “multiple” extension of Hahn–Banach, as observed in [14].

Corollary 5.1.

Let (xi)i=1∞(x_{i})_{i=1}^{\infty} be unit vectors in a normed space XX, (mi)i=1∞(m_{i})_{i=1}^{\infty} real numbers and (wi)i=1∞(w_{i})_{i=1}^{\infty} nonnegative real numbers such that ∑i=1∞wi≤1\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}w_{i}\leq 1. Then there exists a linear functional ϕ∈X∗\phi\in X^{*} with norm at most 11 such that

|ϕ⁡(xi)−mi|≥wi\absolutevalue{\phi(x_i)-m_i}\geq w_{i}

for all ii.

We can also obtain a quantitative improvement of the uniform boundedness principle, or Banach–Steinhaus theorem, which we recall here for the reader’s convenience.

Theorem 5.2.

Let XX be a Banach space, YY a normed space, and Φ\Phi a family of bounded linear operators from XX to YY. If

supϕ∈Φ‖ϕ⁡(x)‖<∞\sup_{\phi\in\Phi}\norm{\phi(x)}<\infty

for all x∈Xx\in X, then

supϕ∈Φ‖ϕ‖<∞.\sup_{\phi\in\Phi}\norm{\phi}<\infty.

It is often useful to consider the contrapositive statement: if a family of bounded linear operators from a Banach space to a normed space is not uniformly bounded, then it is not pointwise bounded. Suppose that we have a family of linear operators on X∗X^{*} that are not uniformly bounded, where XX is a Banach space. Then their operator norm is not bounded and, in particular, the sum ∑n=1∞n​‖ϕn‖−1\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n\norm{\phi_n}^{-1} will be smaller than 11 for some ϕ1,ϕ2,…\phi_{1},\phi_{2},\ldots in this family. But then, Theorem 3.7 with mi=0m_{i}=0 gives a vector xx in the unit ball of XX such that

|ϕn‖ϕn‖​(x)|>n​‖ϕn‖−1\Bigl|\frac{\phi_{n}}{\norm{\phi_n}}(x)\Bigr|>n\norm{\phi_n}^{-1}

for all nn. Rearranging, we get |ϕn​(x)|>n\absolutevalue{\phi_n(x)}>n for all nn, and so our operators are not pointwise bounded. We can push this reasoning much further (see Section 5.2.3).

5.2.2 Plank theorems and linear dynamics

Recall the weak topology on XX is the smallest topology such that every element of the dual space X∗X^{*} is continuous with respect to that topology. We can define weak versions of usual topological notions if they hold with respect to the weak topology. We say a bounded linear operator TT on XX is hypercyclic if there exists x∈Xx\in X such that the orbits Tn(x)=(T∘⋯∘T)(x)T^{n}(x)=(T\circ\cdots\circ T)(x) are dense in XX, and supercyclic if {αTn(x):α∈ℂ,n≥0}\{\alpha T^{n}(x):\alpha\in\mathbb{C},\;n\geq 0\} is dense in XX. If these sets are dense in the weak topology, then we talk about weak hypercyclicity and supercyclicity.

Plank theorems have many connections with linear dynamics. For instance, Ball’s theorems helped in obtaining results on weak hypercyclicity and supercyclicity of operators on Banach and Hilbert spaces, and more generally in answering questions related to the weak topology on Banach spaces (see [21, 47, 85]). Knowing that on infinite-dimensional Banach spaces, the weak and the norm topology do not coincide, here is one simple example of this kind of question.

Question 5.3.

Let (xn)n∈ℕ(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} be a sequence in an infinite-dimensional Banach space XX. Under which condition on xnx_{n} is the set {xn:n∈ℕ}\{x_{n}:n\in\mathbb{N}\} weakly dense in XX?

In general, one can prove that if xnx_{n} is such that ‖xn‖\|x_{n}\| tends to infinity fast enough, then {xn:n∈ℕ}{\{x_{n}:n\in\mathbb{N}\}} is weakly closed in XX, so certainly not weakly dense. Here is a more precise sharp formulation of this idea. The proofs we follow are given in [85, Propositions 5.2–5.4] and [21, Section 10.1.1].

Theorem 5.4.

Let (xn)n∈ℕ(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} be a sequence of nonzero vectors in the Banach space XX. If

∑n=1∞1‖xn‖<∞,\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\|x_{n}\|}<\infty,

then the set {xn:n∈ℕ}\{x_{n}:n\in\mathbb{N}\} is weakly closed in XX. Furthermore, if XX is a real or complex Hilbert space, then it is sufficient that ∑n=1∞‖xn‖−2<∞\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\|x_{n}\|^{-2}<\infty.

Proof.

We only prove the Banach space case here. The proof of the complex Hilbert one is virtually the same, and for the real Hilbert space, one needs to consider the complexification of XX. It will be enough to show that the weak closure of the xnx_{n} does not contain 00 (to see why, replace xnx_{n} with xn−zx_{n}-z, where z∈X∖{xn:n∈ℕ}z\in X\setminus\{x_{n}:n\in\mathbb{N}\}).

Let s:=∑n=1∞‖xn‖−1s:=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\|x_{n}\|^{-1} and αn:=1/s​‖xn‖\alpha_{n}:=1/s\|x_{n}\|, so that ∑n=1∞αn=1\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\alpha_{n}=1. Then Corollary 5.1 with the unit vectors xn/‖xn‖x_{n}/\|x_{n}\| yields a ϕ\phi in X∗X^{*} such that

|ϕ⁡(xn)|≥1s\absolutevalue{\phi(x_n)}\geq\frac{1}{s}

for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. It follows that 00 is not in the weak closure of {xn:n∈ℕ}\{x_{n}:n\in\mathbb{N}\}. ∎

Theorem 5.4 is tight in the sense that it has been shown that if XX is an infinite-dimensional Banach space and (cn)n∈ℕ(c_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} is a sequence of positive numbers such that ∑n=1∞cn−2=∞\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_{n}^{-2}=\infty, then there exists a sequence (xn)n∈ℕ∈X(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in X such that ‖xn‖=cn\|x_{n}\|=c_{n} for all nn and 00 is in the weak closure of {xn:n∈ℕ}\{x_{n}:n\in\mathbb{N}\} (see [85, Proposition 6.11]).

5.2.3 A stronger version of the uniform boundedness principle

While Theorem 5.2 is no longer true if we omit the supremum, one may wonder under what conditions it holds that there is a sequence of bounded linear operators ϕn∈Φ\phi_{n}\in\Phi and some x∈Xx\in X such that ‖ϕn​(x)‖→∞\|\phi_{n}(x)\|\to\infty. This question is intimately related to linear dynamics via the study of orbits of linear operators, hence the first partial results came from searching for conditions ensuring that orbits are going to infinity (see [22] and the book of Beauzamy [23, Chapter III], in particular III.2.C.1 for the following theorem).

Theorem 5.5.

Let TT be an operator on a Hilbert space HH such that

∑n=1∞1‖Tn‖<∞.\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\|T^{n}\|}<\infty.

Then there is a dense set of points x∈Hx\in H such that ‖Tn​x‖→∞\|T^{n}x\|\to\infty as n→∞n\to\infty.

This theorem is not sharp. In fact, it suffices that ∑n=1∞cn​(Tn)2<∞\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_{n}(T^{n})^{2}<\infty for the result to hold, where

cn(Tn):=inf{∥Tn|Z∥:Z⊂X,codimZ<n}c_{n}(T^{n}):=\inf\{\|T^{n}|_{Z}\|:Z\subset X,\>\codim Z<n\}

is the nnth Gelfand number of the operator TnT^{n} (see III.2.C.5 in [23]). The hypotheses of Theorem 5.5 are reminiscent of Theorem 5.4 and the proof relies on Bang’s lemma. It was noted in 19901990 by Beauzamy that a solution to the symmetric plank problem (that is, to Bang’s conjecture for symmetric convex bodies) would extend Theorem 5.5 more generally to a sequence of bounded operators and thus strengthen the uniform boundedness principle. This actually prompted Ball to work on plank problems. We can find a proof of this stenghtening of Theorem 5.5 in a paper of Müller and Vršovský [73] for a single x∈Hx\in H, where the hypotheses for a complex Hilbert space are slightly weakened. It was later showed [72] that the conditions in the following theorem are sufficient to ensure that the set of x∈Xx\in X such that ‖Tn​x‖→∞\norm{T_nx}\to\infty is dense in XX.

Theorem 5.6.

Let TnT_{n}, n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, be a sequence of bounded linear operators on a Banach space XX. If

∑n=1∞1‖Tn‖<∞,\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\norm{T_n}}<\infty,

then there exists x∈Xx\in X such that ‖Tn​x‖→∞\norm{T_nx}\to\infty. Furthermore, if XX is a complex Hilbert space, then it is sufficient that ∑n=1∞‖Tn‖−2<∞\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\norm{T_n}^{-2}<\infty.

Proof.

We treat the case where XX is a complex Hilbert space because the proof is more natural in this setting. A few modifications are needed in the Banach space case (see [73]).

Choose βn\beta_{n} positive real numbers going to infinity such that

s:=∑n=1∞βn‖Tn‖2<∞,s:=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\beta_{n}}{\norm{T_n}^{2}}<\infty,

and define

αn:=1s+1​βn‖Tn‖.\alpha_{n}:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{s+1}}\frac{\sqrt{\beta_{n}}}{\norm{T_n}}.

For all nn, take gn∈X∗g_{n}\in X^{*} such that ‖gn‖≤1\norm{g_n}\leq 1 and ‖Tn∗​gn‖≥‖Tn∗‖/2=‖Tn‖/2\norm{T_n^*g_n}\geq\norm{T_n^*}/2=\norm{T_n}/2. Finally, define

fn:=Tn∗​gn‖Tn∗​gn‖∈X∗.f_{n}:=\frac{T_{n}^{*}g_{n}}{\norm{T_n^*g_n}}\in X^{*}.

We can apply Theorem 4.1 with these linear functionals. Indeed, since the coefficients αn\alpha_{n} satisfy

∑n=1∞αn2=s​(s+1)−1<1,\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\alpha_{n}^{2}=s(s+1)^{-1}<1,

we know there exists x∈Xx\in X with ‖x‖=1\norm{x}=1 and |⟨x,fn⟩|≥αn\absolutevalue{\inner{x}{f_n}}\geq\alpha_{n} for all nn. Then,

‖Tn​x‖≥‖Tn​x‖​‖gn‖≥|⟨Tn​x,gn⟩|=|⟨x,Tn∗​gn⟩|=‖Tn∗​gn‖​|⟨x,fn⟩|≥‖Tn‖2​αn.\norm{T_nx}\geq\norm{T_nx}\norm{g_n}\geq\absolutevalue{\inner{T_nx}{g_n}}=\absolutevalue{\inner{x}{T_n^*g_n}}=\norm{T_n^*g_n}\absolutevalue{\inner{x}{f_n}}\geq\frac{\norm{T_n}}{2}\alpha_{n}.

This expression simplifies to βn/2​s+1\sqrt{\beta_{n}}/2\sqrt{s+1} and thus tends to ∞\infty with nn by our choice of βn\beta_{n}. ∎

We end this section by noting that Theorem 5.6 is optimal in the sense that there exists a Banach space XX and operators TnT_{n} such that

∑n=1∞1‖Tn‖1+ε<∞,\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\norm{T_n}^{1+\varepsilon}}<\infty,

yet there is no x∈Xx\in X with ‖Tn​x‖→∞\norm{T_n x}\to\infty. An explicit construction is given in [73].

5.3 Applications in harmonic analysis

The Riemann–Lebesgue lemma says that the Fourier coefficients of an L1​(𝕋)L_{1}(\mathbb{T}) function tend to 00 as |n|→∞\absolutevalue{n}\to\infty, where 𝕋\mathbb{T} stands for the unit circle. It is natural to wonder how fast this happens. In particular, can this decay be arbitrarily slow? Kolmogorov answered this question positively in 1923. More precisely, he showed that for any choice of sequence of positive integers (an)n∈ℤ(a_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} with an→0a_{n}\to 0 as |n|→∞\absolutevalue{n}\to\infty, there exists a function f∈L1​(𝕋)f\in L_{1}(\mathbb{T}) such that f^​(n)≥an\widehat{f}(n)\geq a_{n} for all nn. A similar problem, asking whether all square summable sequences are dominated by the Fourier coefficients of some continuous function on the unit circle 𝕋\mathbb{T}, turned out to be much harder to settle. Fortunately, the mathematicians de Leeuw, Kahane, and Katznelson [44] were able to provide a positive answer in 1977. They even showed that we may take this function to be bounded on 𝕋\mathbb{T}. You can think of their result as saying that we cannot distinguish functions in L2​(𝕋)L_{2}(\mathbb{T}) from functions in C⁡(𝕋)C(\mathbb{T}) if we only look at the size of their Fourier coefficients.

Theorem 5.7.

Let (an)n∈ℤ∈ℓ2​(ℤ)(a_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\in\ell_{2}(\mathbb{Z}). Then there exists f∈C⁡(𝕋)f\in C(\mathbb{T}) and an absolute constant A>0A>0 such that ‖f‖∞≤A​(∑n∈ℤ|an|2)1/2\norm{f}_{\infty}\leq A\left(\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\absolutevalue{a_n}^{2}\right)^{1/2} and

|f^​(n)|≥|an||\widehat{f}(n)|\geq\absolutevalue{a_n}

for all nn.

What is surprising with the proof of this theorem is that it considers sums of the form

∑i=1∞ϵi​ai​ψi,\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\epsilon_{i}a_{i}\psi_{i},

where (ψn)n=1∞(\psi_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty} is a sequence of functions and (ϵn)n=1∞(\epsilon_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty} is a random choice of signs, which is reminiscent of Bang’s lemma once again. See the beginning of the proof of Theorem 5.8 below for an explicit example of how this kind of sum might appear.

We can go further with these ideas and ask: Given a sequence of functions ψn∈L1​(𝕋)\psi_{n}\in L_{1}(\mathbb{T}), under which conditions can we guarantee that there exists a bounded function ff such that

|⟨f,ψn⟩|>|an|\absolutevalue{\inner{f}{\psi_n}}>\absolutevalue{a_n}

for any sequence (an)n=1∞∈ℓ2​(ℤ)(a_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\in\ell_{2}(\mathbb{Z})? Unfortunately, the de Leeuw–Kahane–Katznelson theorem does not answer this question in general. However, many years later, a theorem of Nazarov solved this problem and it was proven using ideas coming from plank theorems. This is self-evident upon reading the title of Nazarov’s paper: The Bang solution of the coefficient problem [74]. In fact, according to Nazarov himself, the modification in the demonstration of Bang’s result needed to prove the following theorem was so minor that he claimed, “[…] I actually even do not pretend to be an author of the next two sections; rather I act there like a shadow that enters and goes over many strange places which completely eliminate the attention of his master just passing by.” We remark that Nazarov’s original article is in Russian, but an English translation is available [74].

Theorem 5.8.

Let TT be a probability space with measure μ\mu and (ψn)n=1∞(\psi_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty} a sequence of unit functionals in T∗T^{*} such that

‖∑i=1∞ci​ψi‖2≤(∑i=1∞ci2)1/2\Bigl\|\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}c_{i}\psi_{i}\Bigr\|_{2}\leq\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}c_{i}^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2} (5.6)

for all sequences of real coefficients (cn)n=1∞(c_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}. For 2≤p≤∞2\leq p\leq\infty and qq its conjugate exponent, suppose that

‖ψn‖q≥β>0\norm{\psi_n}_{q}\geq\beta>0 (5.7)

for all nn. Let aia_{i} be positive numbers such that ∑i=1∞ai2=1\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}a_{i}^{2}=1. Then there exists F∈Lp​(T)F\in L_{p}(T) such that

‖F‖p≤(3​π2)1−2/p​β−2\norm{F}_{p}\leq\Bigl(\frac{3\pi}{2}\Bigr)^{1-2/p}\beta^{-2}

and, for all nn,

|⟨F,ψn⟩|≥an.\absolutevalue{\inner{F}{\psi_n}}\geq a_{n}.
Proof.

For a choice of signs ϵ=(ϵi)i=1∞\epsilon=(\epsilon_{i})_{i=1}^{\infty}, let

fϵ:=∑i=1∞ϵi​ai​ψi,f_{\epsilon}:=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\epsilon_{i}a_{i}\psi_{i},

and note that from (5.6) and the assumption ∑i=1∞ai2=1\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}a_{i}^{2}=1, it follows that fϵ∈L2​(T)f_{\epsilon}\in L_{2}(T) (more precisely, ‖fϵ‖2≤1\norm{f_\epsilon}_{2}\leq 1 for all ϵ\epsilon). Theorems of existence and uniqueness of ODEs allow us to define the (unique) function Φ\Phi by the initial conditions Φ⁡(0)=Φ′​(0)=0\Phi(0)=\Phi^{\prime}(0)=0 and the differential equation

Φ′′​(x)=(1+x2)2/p−1.\Phi^{\prime\prime}(x)=(1+x^{2})^{2/p-1}.

From the definition of Φ\Phi, the integral I⁡(f):=∫TΦ⁡(f)​𝑑μI(f):=\int_{T}\Phi(f)\,d\mu is well-defined and continuous in L2​(T)L_{2}(T). Moreover, since {fϵ}\{f_{\epsilon}\} is compact in the topology of L2​(T)L_{2}(T), the integral attains a maximum for some fϵ¯f_{\overline{\epsilon}}. The FF we pick will be a rescaling of Φ′​(fϵ¯)\Phi^{\prime}(f_{\overline{\epsilon}}), so let us start by showing that Φ′​(fϵ¯)∈Lp​(T)\Phi^{\prime}(f_{\overline{\epsilon}})\in L_{p}(T). By the definition of Φ⁡(x)\Phi(x) and Hölder’s inequality,

|Φ′​(x)|=|∫0x(1+t2)2/p−1​𝑑t|≤∫0|x|(1+t2)2/p−1​𝑑t≤(∫0|x|𝑑t)2/p​(∫0|x|(1+t2)−1​𝑑t)1−2/p.\displaystyle\absolutevalue{\Phi'(x)}=\Bigl|\int_{0}^{x}(1+t^{2})^{2/p-1}\,dt\Bigr|\leq\int_{0}^{|x|}(1+t^{2})^{2/p-1}\,dt\leq\Bigl(\int_{0}^{|x|}\,dt\Bigr)^{2/p}\Bigl(\int_{0}^{|x|}(1+t^{2})^{-1}\,dt\Bigr)^{1-2/p}.

These integrals evaluate to |x|2/p​(arctan⁡|x|)1−2/p≤|x|2/p​(π/2)1−2/p|x|^{2/p}(\arctan|x|)^{1-2/p}\leq|x|^{2/p}(\pi/2)^{1-2/p}, so that

‖Φ′​(fϵ¯)‖p≤(π2)1−2/p​(∫T|fϵ¯|2​𝑑μ)1/p≤(π2)1−2/p,\norm{\Phi'(f_{\overline{\epsilon}})}_{p}\leq\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{1-2/p}\Bigl(\int_{T}|f_{\overline{\epsilon}}|^{2}\,d\mu\Bigr)^{1/p}\leq\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{1-2/p},

using our previous observation that ‖fϵ‖2≤1\norm{f_{\epsilon}}_{2}\leq 1 for all ϵ\epsilon. Furthermore, we see that upon taking F:=31−2/p​β−2​Φ′​(fϵ¯)F:=3^{1-2/p}\beta^{-2}\Phi^{\prime}(f_{\overline{\epsilon}}), we have

‖F‖p≤(3​π2)1−2/p​β−2,\norm{F}_{p}\leq\Bigl(\frac{3\pi}{2}\Bigr)^{1-2/p}\beta^{-2},

as desired.

Now we want to show that for all jj,

aj≤|⟨F,ψj⟩|=31−2/p​β−2​|∫TΦ′​(fϵ¯)​ψj​𝑑μ|.a_{j}\leq\absolutevalue{\inner{F}{\psi_j}}=3^{1-2/p}\beta^{-2}\Bigl|\int_{T}\Phi^{\prime}(f_{\overline{\epsilon}})\psi_{j}\,d\mu\Bigr|. (5.8)

For each jj, let fj:=fϵ¯−2​ϵ¯j​aj​ψjf_{j}:=f_{\overline{\epsilon}}-2\overline{\epsilon}_{j}a_{j}\psi_{j}, that is, flip the sign of the jjth term in the sum defining fϵ¯f_{\overline{\epsilon}}. Since fϵ¯f_{\overline{\epsilon}} maximizes I⁡(⋅)I(\cdot), we have 0≤∫T(Φ⁡(fϵ¯)−Φ⁡(fj))​𝑑μ0\leq\int_{T}(\Phi(f_{\overline{\epsilon}})-\Phi(f_{j}))\;d\mu for each jj, and by the mean value theorem, there exists a function gg between fjf_{j} and fϵ¯f_{\overline{\epsilon}} such that

∫T(Φ⁡(fϵ¯)−Φ⁡(fj))​𝑑μ\displaystyle\int_{T}(\Phi(f_{\overline{\epsilon}})-\Phi(f_{j}))\;d\mu =∫T(Φ′​(fϵ¯)​(fϵ¯−fj)+12​Φ′′​(g)​(fϵ¯−fj)2)​𝑑μ\displaystyle=\int_{T}\Bigl(\Phi^{\prime}(f_{\overline{\epsilon}})(f_{\overline{\epsilon}}-f_{j})+\frac{1}{2}\Phi^{\prime\prime}(g)(f_{\overline{\epsilon}}-f_{j})^{2}\Bigr)\,d\mu
=2​aj​∫TΦ′​(fϵ¯)​ϵ¯j​ψj+2​aj2​∫TΦ′′​(g)​ψj2​𝑑μ.\displaystyle=2a_{j}\int_{T}\Phi^{\prime}(f_{\overline{\epsilon}})\overline{\epsilon}_{j}\psi_{j}+2a_{j}^{2}\int_{T}\Phi^{\prime\prime}(g)\psi_{j}^{2}\,d\mu.

Since fϵ¯−fj=2​ϵ¯j​aj​ψjf_{\overline{\epsilon}}-f_{j}=2\overline{\epsilon}_{j}a_{j}\psi_{j}, we have

0≤2​aj​∫TΦ′​(fϵ¯)​ϵ¯j​ψj+2​aj2​∫TΦ′′​(g)​ψj2​𝑑μ,0\leq 2a_{j}\int_{T}\Phi^{\prime}(f_{\overline{\epsilon}})\overline{\epsilon}_{j}\psi_{j}+2a_{j}^{2}\int_{T}\Phi^{\prime\prime}(g)\psi_{j}^{2}\,d\mu,

whence

|∫TΦ′​(fϵ¯)​ψj​𝑑μ|≥aj​∫TΦ′′​(g)​ψj2​𝑑μ.\Bigl|\int_{T}\Phi^{\prime}(f_{\overline{\epsilon}})\psi_{j}\;d\mu\Bigr|\geq a_{j}\int_{T}\Phi^{\prime\prime}(g)\psi_{j}^{2}\;d\mu.

These previous steps are reminiscent of the strategy adopted in the proof of Bang’s lemma.

We see from (5.8) that we will be done if we can show that ∫TΦ′′​(g)​ψj2​𝑑μ≥32/p−1​β2.\int_{T}\Phi^{\prime\prime}(g)\psi_{j}^{2}\;d\mu\geq 3^{2/p-1}\beta^{2}. Since q2+(1−2p)​q2=1\frac{q}{2}+(1-\frac{2}{p})\frac{q}{2}=1, Hölder’s inequality gives

(∫T(1+g2)​𝑑μ)1−q/2​(∫T(1+g2)2/p−1​ψj2​𝑑μ)q/2≥∫T|ψj|q≥βq,\Bigl(\int_{T}(1+g^{2})\;d\mu\Bigr)^{1-q/2}\Bigl(\int_{T}(1+g^{2})^{2/p-1}\psi_{j}^{2}\;d\mu\Bigr)^{q/2}\geq\int_{T}\absolutevalue{\psi_j}^{q}\geq\beta^{q},

where we used (5.7) to obtain the last inequality. Since gg lies between fjf_{j} and fϵ¯f_{\overline{\epsilon}}, we have g2≤fj2+fϵ¯2g^{2}\leq f_{j}^{2}+f_{\overline{\epsilon}}^{2} and thus ∫T(1+g2)​𝑑μ≤∫T(1+fj2+fϵ¯2)​𝑑μ≤3\int_{T}(1+g^{2})\;d\mu\leq\int_{T}(1+f_{j}^{2}+f_{\overline{\epsilon}}^{2})\;d\mu\leq 3, using that ‖fϵ‖2≤1\norm{f_{\epsilon}}_{2}\leq 1 for all ϵ\epsilon. We conclude that

∫TΦ′′​(g)​ψj2​𝑑μ=∫T(1+g2)​ψj2​𝑑μ≥31−2/q​β2=32/p−1​β2.∎\int_{T}\Phi^{\prime\prime}(g)\psi_{j}^{2}\;d\mu=\int_{T}(1+g^{2})\psi_{j}^{2}\;d\mu\geq 3^{1-2/q}\beta^{2}=3^{2/p-1}\beta^{2}.\qed

The following corollary of Nazarov’s theorem gives a more direct answer to the coefficient problem. It follows from the p=∞p=\infty case of Theorem 5.8 and an application of a weak form of Grothendieck’s inequality (see [17], a paper of Ball that talks about Nazarov’s theorem, among other things).

Corollary 5.9.

Let (ψn)n=1∞(\psi_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty} be functions of norm 11 in L1​(𝕋)L_{1}(\mathbb{T}) such that there exists a constant M>0M>0 with

‖∑i=1∞ci​ψi‖1≤M​(∑i=1∞ci2)1/2\Bigl\|\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}c_{i}\psi_{i}\Bigr\|_{1}\leq M\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}c_{i}^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2}

for all sequences of real coefficients (cn)n=1∞(c_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}. Then, for all (an)n=1∞∈ℓ2​(ℤ)(a_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\in\ell_{2}(\mathbb{Z}), there exists a bounded function ff such that

|⟨f,ψn⟩|>|an|\absolutevalue{\inner{f}{\psi_n}}>|a_{n}|

for all nn.

5.3.1 Applications and extensions of Nazarov’s result

The coefficient problem is intimately related to applied problems via the Fourier transform, and so Nazarov’s result has recently attracted attention in signal processing and electrical engineering. For instance, an important mathematical problem in computational imaging is to develop optimal coded apertures. In [1], their fundamental limits were characterized using Theorem 5.8, and a greedy algorithm that relies on the proof of this theorem was proposed. Also see [34] for a discussion of various problems in signal processing where Theorem 5.8 might come in handy. In particular, observe that Theorem 5.8 does not require orthogonality of the unit functionals, but only asks for an ℓ2\ell_{2} estimate, hence it can be used in problems regarding frames and bases in more generality.

Both the results of de Leeuw, Kahane, and Katznelson, and Nazarov, give insight on the spectral structure of large sets in additive combinatorics, as observed for example in works of Green [55]. Here, for a function f:ℤ/N​ℤ→ℂf:\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C} and r∈ℤ/N​ℤr\in\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}, the Fourier transform of ff at rr is defined as

f^​(r)=∑xf⁡(x)​e​(r​x/N),\widehat{f}(r)=\sum_{x}f(x)e(rx/N),

where e⁡(x)=exp⁡(2​π​i​x)e(x)=\exp(2\pi ix). As mentioned by Green, the result of Nazarov implies that the only information we can obtain on the large spectrum of a large subset of ℤ/N​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z} comes from Parseval’s theorem (via Chang’s theorem, see [55] for more details and the following result).

Theorem 5.10.

Let αr\alpha_{r}, r∈ℤ/N​ℤr\in\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}, be positive reals satisfying ∑rαr2≤N/1600{\sum_{r}\alpha_{r}^{2}\leq N/1600}. Then there is a function f:ℤ/N​ℤ→[0,1]f:\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}\to[0,1] such that |f|=∑xf⁡(x)=N/2|f|=\sum_{x}f(x)=N/2, and so that

|f^​(r)|≥αr​|f||\widehat{f}(r)|\geq\alpha_{r}|f|

for all r∈ℤ/N​ℤr\in\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}.

Finally, we want to highlight the fact that soon after Nazarov’s result, Lust-Piquard [66] obtained noncommutative versions of the de Leeuw–Kahane–Katznelson and Nazarov theorems. In particular, the reader is invited to compare Theorem 5.7 with the following statement, where we say that a matrix AA is in ℓ∞​(ℓ2)\ell_{\infty}(\ell_{2}) if ‖A‖ℓ∞​(ℓ2)2=supi∑j|ai​j|2<∞.\|A\|_{\ell_{\infty}(\ell_{2})}^{2}=\sup_{i}\sum_{j}\absolutevalue{a_{ij}}^{2}<\infty.

Theorem 5.11.

Let AA be such that AA and A∗A^{*} are in ℓ∞​(ℓ2)\ell_{\infty}(\ell_{2}). Then there exists a matrix BB that defines a bounded operator from ℓ2\ell_{2} to ℓ2\ell_{2} such that

‖B‖ℓ2→ℓ2≤6​max⁡{‖A‖ℓ∞​(ℓ2),‖A∗‖ℓ∞​(ℓ2)}\norm{B}_{\ell_{2}\to\ell_{2}}\leq\sqrt{6}\max\{\norm{A}_{\ell_{\infty}(\ell_{2})},\norm{A^*}_{\ell_{\infty}(\ell_{2})}\}

and |bi​j|≥|ai​j|\absolutevalue{b_{ij}}\geq\absolutevalue{a_{ij}} for all i,j≥0i,j\geq 0. Moreover, the constant 6\sqrt{6} is best possible.

In the previous result, it is possible to replace ℓ2→ℓ2\ell_{2}\to\ell_{2} with other spaces ℓp→ℓq\ell_{p}\to\ell_{q} modulo minor modifications.

It is interesting to note that this theorem was a central element in a new proof [43] of a well-known result of Varopoulos on a characterization of Schur multipliers, which are bounded operators from ℓ2→ℓ2\ell_{2}\to\ell_{2} that act by entrywise multiplication with a matrix. The following is a restatement of Varopoulos’s result to resemble Theorem 5.11.

Theorem 5.12.

Let 𝒮⁡(A)\mathscr{S}(A) be the set of symbols with matrix entries bi​jb_{ij} satisfying |bi​j|≤|ai​j||b_{ij}|\leq|a_{ij}|. Then the following are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    every symbol in 𝒮⁡(A)\mathscr{S}(A) defines a Schur multiplier;

  2. 2.

    we can write A=C+DA=C+D where C∈ℓ∞​(ℓ2)C\in\ell_{\infty}(\ell_{2}) and D∗∈ℓ∞​(ℓ2)D^{*}\in\ell_{\infty}(\ell_{2});

  3. 3.

    for all finite sets of indices II and JJ,

    ∑i∈I∑j∈J|ai​j|2=O⁡(|I|+|J|).\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}|a_{ij}|^{2}=O(|I|+|J|).

6 Applications in number theory

In this section, we present some applications of plank theorems in number theory. It is interesting to note that alternatively, number theory can sometimes give insight into plank problems. For instance, letting the height of a point (x1,⋯,xn)(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n}) be max1≤i≤n⁡|xi|\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|x_{i}|, Fukshansky [50] used his bounds on the height of integral points of small height outside a hypersurface defined by a nonzero integer polynomial over ℚ\mathbb{Q} to obtain a lower bound for a discrete plank problem which concerns coverings of the set of integer lattice points in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} contained in a cube by sublattices of rank d−1d-1. See Section 4.4.1 for a discussion on discrete analogues of plank problems.

6.1 Simultaneous Diophantine approximation and piercing convex bodies

Recall the classical result of Dirichlet in Diophantine approximation which states that for all real θ\theta, there exist infinitely many natural numbers qq such that

‖q​θ‖≤1q,\norm{q\theta}\leq\frac{1}{q},

where ‖⋅‖\norm{\cdot} denotes the distance to the nearest integer. We say that θ\theta is badly approximable if the right-hand side of the previous inequality cannot be improved by any positive constant, that is, if there exists c=c⁡(θ)>0c=c(\theta)>0 such that ‖q​θ‖>c​q−1\norm{q\theta}>cq^{-1} for all q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N}. The set of badly approximable numbers has Lebesgue measure zero, but full Hausdorff dimension. These numbers are also closely related to Littlewood’s conjecture, a famous and long-standing open problem in Diophantine approximation, which says that if θ,φ∈ℝ\theta,\varphi\in\mathbb{R}, then

lim infn→∞n​‖n​θ‖​‖n​φ‖=0.\liminf_{n\to\infty}n\norm{n\theta}\norm{n\varphi}=0.

Since there is also a simultaneous Diophantine approximation theorem which states that for any θ,φ∈ℝ\theta,\varphi\in\mathbb{R}, there exist infinitely many q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N} such that

max⁡{‖q​θ‖2,‖q​φ‖2}≤1q,\max\{\norm{q\theta}^{2},\norm{q\varphi}^{2}\}\leq\frac{1}{q},

it is natural to define a pair of badly approximable numbers as a pair of reals θ,φ\theta,\varphi such that there exists a positive constant c=c⁡(θ,φ)c=c(\theta,\varphi) which verifies

max⁡{‖q​θ‖2,‖q​φ‖2}>cq\max\{\norm{q\theta}^{2},\norm{q\varphi}^{2}\}>\frac{c}{q}

for all q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N}. Davenport showed that the set of these pairs is uncountable, and it was later shown that in fact, it has Hausdorff dimension two. Davenport [41] also proved the following related theorem on simultaneous Diophantine approximation.

Theorem 6.1.

Let (λi)i=1n(\lambda_{i})_{i=1}^{n} and (μi)i=1n(\mu_{i})_{i=1}^{n} be real numbers. Then there exist α\alpha and β\beta such that α+λi\alpha+\lambda_{i} and β+μi\beta+\mu_{i} form a pair of badly approximable numbers for i=1,2,…,ni=1,2,\ldots,n. Furthermore, we may take the constant c=2−4​n−7c=2^{-4n-7} in the definition of a pair of badly approximable numbers.

This result has connections with convex geometry since Davenport’s solution uses geometric arguments. More precisely, he proves by induction the existence of a square in the plane such that all points (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) in that square satisfy the requirements of the theorem. The generalization to higher dimensions and to simultaneous Diophantine approximation of many reals is immediate. We can also infer from this result another type of geometric pigeonhole principle [4].

Theorem 6.2.

Let CC be a cube in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and (Hi)i=1n(H_{i})_{i=1}^{n} hyperplanes. Then we can find in CC another cube having the same orientation, being at least 2−n2^{-n} times as wide as CC, and such that none of the HiH_{i} intersect its interior.

As mentioned in Section 2.2.3, Alexander already observed that a positive answer to Bang’s conjecture would improve the previous theorem. As such, Theorem 3.2 also improves it and, in particular, implies that for a symmetric convex body CC, we can find a set that does not intersect any of the hyperplanes HiH_{i} via a well-chosen dilation and translation of CC [14].

Corollary 6.3.

Let CC be a symmetric convex body in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and (Hi)i=1n(H_{i})_{i=1}^{n} hyperplanes. Then there exists a vector xx such that x+1n+1​Cx+\frac{1}{n+1}C is in CC and such that none of the HiH_{i} intersect the interior of x+1n+1​Cx+\frac{1}{n+1}C.

We follow the proof from [14].

Proof.

Without loss of generality, we take CC centered at the origin. Recall that CC being a symmetric convex body, it is the unit ball of some finite-dimensional normed space, so it makes sense to define XX such that CC corresponds to its unit ball. Consider the unit functionals ϕi∈X∗\phi_{i}\in X^{*} and the real numbers mim_{i} that correspond to the hyperplanes

Hi={x∈ℝd:ϕi​(x)=mi}.H_{i}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\phi_{i}(x)=m_{i}\}.

Theorem 3.2 gives x′∈Cx^{\prime}\in C such that

|ϕi​(x′)−n+1n​mi|≥1/n.\Bigl|\phi_{i}(x^{\prime})-\frac{n+1}{n}m_{i}\Bigr|\geq 1/n.

Changing the scale by a factor of n/(n+1)n/(n+1), we have an x∈nn+1​C\displaystyle x\in\frac{n}{n+1}C, explicitly x=nn+1​x′\displaystyle x=\frac{n}{n+1}x^{\prime}, such that

|ϕi​(x)−mi|≥1n+1\absolutevalue{\phi_i(x)-m_i}\geq\frac{1}{n+1} (6.1)

for all ii, and x+1n+1​C⊆C\displaystyle x+\frac{1}{n+1}C\subseteq C. We just have to show that int​(x+1n+1​C)\displaystyle\text{int}\bigl(x+\frac{1}{n+1}C\bigr) will not be sliced by any of the HiH_{i}. For y∈int​(x+1n+1​C)\displaystyle y\in\text{int}\bigl(x+\frac{1}{n+1}C\bigr), we have ‖y−x‖≤(n+1)−1\norm{y-x}\leq(n+1)^{-1}, whence

|ϕi​(y)−mi−(ϕi​(x)−mi)|=|ϕi​(y−x)|≤‖ϕi‖​‖y−x‖≤1n+1.\absolutevalue{\phi_i(y)-m_i-(\phi_i(x)-m_i)}=\absolutevalue{\phi_i(y-x)}\leq\norm{\phi_i}\norm{y-x}\leq\frac{1}{n+1}.

Combining with (6.1), we see that ϕi​(x)−mi\phi_{i}(x)-m_{i} and ϕi​(y)−mi\phi_{i}(y)-m_{i} have the same (nonzero) sign, and in particular ϕi​(y)≠mi\phi_{i}(y)\neq m_{i}. The claim follows. ∎

Corollary 6.3 is intimately related to a recent study on intersecting and piercing all the cells of the n×nn\times n chessboard QnQ_{n} embedded in [−1,1]2[-1,1]^{2}. These cells are explicitly given by

ci​j=[−1+(i−1)⋅2n,−1+i⋅2n]×[−1+(j−1)⋅2n,−1+j⋅2n]c_{ij}=\biggl[-1+(i-1)\cdot\frac{2}{n},-1+i\cdot\frac{2}{n}\biggr]\times\biggl[-1+(j-1)\cdot\frac{2}{n},-1+j\cdot\frac{2}{n}\biggr]

for i,j∈{1,…,n}i,j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}. Here by a line ℓ\ell intersecting (respectively, piercing) a cell ci​jc_{ij}, we mean that ℓ∩ci​j≠∅\ell\cap c_{ij}\neq\emptyset (respectively, ℓ∩int​ci​j≠∅\ell\cap\text{int}\>c_{ij}\neq\emptyset). The authors of [9] conjectured that the minimum number of lines needed to pierce all the cells of QnQ_{n} (call it pnp_{n}) is n−1n-1 for all n≥3n\geq 3, which can be seen as a strengthening of the planar case of the previous corollary for lattice cells. By the same token, it would be an improvement of Ball’s plank theorem for integer points. While only the bounds pn>0.7​np_{n}>0.7n for nn sufficiently large and pn≤n−1p_{n}\leq n-1 for n≥3n\geq 3 were obtained, studying the minimum number of lines needed to intersect all the cells of QnQ_{n} is easier but still related to the plank theorem of Ball. In fact, it is an essential ingredient in proving the following [9].

Proposition 6.4.

For all n≥1n\geq 1, the minimum number of lines needed to intersect all the cells of QnQ_{n} is ⌈n2⌉\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil.

Proof.

Write hnh_{n} for the minimum number of lines needed to intersect all the cells of QnQ_{n}. By picking every second line separating the columns of QnQ_{n}, it is immediate that hn≤⌈n2⌉h_{n}\leq\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil (Fig. 8 serves as a visual aid).

For the lower bound, suppose for a contradiction that the lines ℓ1,…,ℓ⌈n2⌉−1\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil-1} intersect all the cells of QnQ_{n}. Call uiu_{i} the unit normal vector to ℓi\ell_{i} and let XX be ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} endowed with the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty}-norm. For each nonzero u∈ℝ2u\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, define a unit linear functional ϕu\phi_{u} by

ϕu​(x)=⟨x,u⟩‖u‖1.\phi_{u}(x)=\frac{\left\langle x,u\right\rangle}{\|u\|_{1}}.

Then we have an explicit description of the lines (hyperplanes) ℓi\ell_{i} as

ℓi={x∈ℝ2:ϕui​(x)=ti}\ell_{i}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:\phi_{u_{i}}(x)=t_{i}\}

for some ti∈ℝt_{i}\in\mathbb{R}. We apply Ball’s Theorem 3.2 with equal widths 2/n+ϵ2/n+\epsilon, where ϵ>0\epsilon>0 is chosen such that

(⌈n2⌉−1)​(2n+ϵ)=1,\Bigl(\Bigl\lceil\frac{n}{2}\Bigr\rceil-1\Bigr)\Bigl(\frac{2}{n}+\epsilon\Bigr)=1,

thus satisfying the requirement of the theorem. It follows that there is some xx in the unit ball of XX (namely, in [−1,1]2[-1,1]^{2}) with

|ϕui​(x)−ti|≥2n+ϵ|\phi_{u_{i}}(x)-t_{i}|\geq\frac{2}{n}+\epsilon (6.2)

for each ii. Since |ϕui​(x)−ti|≤w|\phi_{u_{i}}(x)-t_{i}|\leq w is equivalent to xx being in the union of all closed squares with edge length 2​w2w and center on ℓi\ell_{i}, we see that (6.2) means that there is an open square centered in [−1,1]2[-1,1]^{2} and with side lengths strictly greater than 4/n4/n that is not intersected by any of the ℓi\ell_{i}, yet every such square must contain a cell of QnQ_{n} (recall the definition of ci​jc_{ij}). This is a contradiction. ∎

We remark that a higher dimensional analogue of Proposition 6.4 holds, and with virtually the same proof, in the sense that the number of hyperplanes needed to intersect each cell of the dd-dimensional box QndQ_{n}^{d} is ⌈n2⌉\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil (see [9]).

6.2 Sphere packings

Recall from Section 4.4.1 the definition of a lattice of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Geometrically, a lattice can be thought of as a regular paving of Euclidean space. The study of lattices connects convex geometry and number theory. For instance, Ball [15] saw a link between sphere packings and Bang’s lemma after working on his plank theorems. This allowed him to obtain the asymptotically best lower bound on the density of sphere packings in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} at the time. This has subsequently been improved by a constant factor in large dimensions [88] and, very recently, by a factor of log⁡n\log n [38] and of nn [61]. But what is of particular interest to us is his novel approach rather than the exact expression for the lower bound itself, so we shall describe it now.

Many of the upper bounds on sphere packing densities are obtained via a lattice packing in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, namely a family of balls of the same radius in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with centers on the coordinates of a lattice and with disjoint interiors. Its density is the proportion of space covered by this lattice packing. A classical result of Minkowski (see [57]) says that for all nn, we can find a sphere packing in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with density at least 21−n​ζ​(n)2^{1-n}\zeta(n), where ζ⁡(n)=∑k=1∞k−n\zeta(n)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}k^{-n} is the Riemann zeta function, but you can think of ζ⁡(n)\zeta(n) as some term tending to 11 from above with nn. The best result for a long time was from Davenport and Rogers [42] and indicated a lower bound of roughly 1,68⋅n​2−n1,68\cdot n2^{-n}. Here is Ball’s improvement to this lower bound.

Theorem 6.5.

For all n≥1n\geq 1, there exists a sphere packing in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} having density greater than or equal to 2​(n−1)​2−n​ζ​(n)2(n-1)2^{-n}\zeta(n).

It is straightforward to compare the three previous lower bounds for different values of nn. Note that Ball did not fully justify the apparition of ζ⁡(n)\zeta(n) in his result, because this term appears naturally after using Möbius inversion (which can be thought of as the identity ∑d|nμ⁡(d)=1\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)=1 when n=1n=1 and 00 otherwise) and the formula ∑k=1∞μ⁡(k)​k−n=ζ​(n)−1\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\mu(k)k^{-n}=\zeta(n)^{-1} (it is, in fact, the same argument that Minkowski used). Here, the Möbius function μ⁡(n)\mu(n) is supported on squarefree integers, and on these integers it is defined by μ⁡(1)=1\mu(1)=1 and μ⁡(n)=(−1)r\mu(n)=(-1)^{r} if nn has rr distinct prime factors.

We present here the arguments of Ball that make use of the ideas of plank theorems and we only sketch the other arguments. A few remarks will first allow us to simplify the proof.

Remark 6.6.

The determinant of a lattice is an invariant defined as the absolute value of the determinant of the matrix representation of the linear isomorphism between this lattice and ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}. In particular, the density of a sphere packing of volume VV in LL is V/det⁡LV/\det L. Moreover, we say that a lattice LL is admissible with respect to a symmetric convex body CC if the only point of LL that the interior of CC contains is 00. Take CC to be the ball of radius 2​r2r centered at 00. Then a lattice LL contains a sphere packing of balls of radius rr if and only if LL is admissible with respect to CC. Without loss of generality, we will be looking for a lattice with determinant 11, so that its density coincides with the volume of the balls in the sphere packing. Hence, Ball’s result with follow if we find a determinant 11 lattice that is admissible for the ball of volume 2​(n−1)2(n-1) centered at 00. But by a compactness argument, it suffices to find a family of determinant 11 lattices that are admissible for the ball of volume ≥2​(n−1)−o​(1)\geq 2(n-1)-o(1). Equivalently, we can fix the lattice to be ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} and find origin-centered admissible ellipsoids of volume

Vol​(ER)≥2​(n−1)−o⁡(1)\text{Vol}(E_{R})\geq 2(n-1)-o(1) (6.3)

as R→∞R\to\infty. Here, by origin-centered ellipsoids, we mean deformations of the standard unit ball B1={x∈ℝn:‖x‖2≤1}B_{1}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\|x\|^{2}\leq 1\} under a linear transformation. The volume of an ellipsoid E=L⁡(B1)E=L(B_{1}) is Vol​(E)=det⁡Q⋅Vol​(B1)\text{Vol}(E)=\sqrt{\det Q}\cdot\text{Vol}(B_{1}), where Q=L​LTQ=LL^{T}.

Proof of Theorem 6.5.

Define the ellipsoids ERE_{R} mentioned in Remark 6.6 by the equation

⟨u,x⟩2+‖x‖2≤R2\left\langle u,x\right\rangle^{2}+\norm{x}^{2}\leq R^{2} (6.4)

for x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and u=u⁡(R)u=u(R) to be chosen to satisfy the inequality (6.3). From our Remark 6.6, the volume of ERE_{R} is simply

Vol​(ER)=11+K2​Vol​(BR),\text{Vol}(E_{R})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+K^{2}}}\text{Vol}(B_{R}), (6.5)

where K=K⁡(R)K=K(R) is the length of uu and BRB_{R} the ball of radius RR centered at the origin. Moreover 1+K2=K+o⁡(1)\sqrt{1+K^{2}}=K+o(1) as R→∞R\to\infty, since then the length of uu will also tend to infinity. It will thus suffice to show that

KVol​(BR)≤12​(n−1)+o⁡(1)\frac{K}{\text{Vol}(B_{R})}\leq\frac{1}{2(n-1)}+o(1) (6.6)

as R→∞R\to\infty.

By the definition of an admissible lattice, ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} is admissible for ERE_{R} if

⟨u,z⟩2+‖z‖2≥R2\left\langle u,z\right\rangle^{2}+\norm{z}^{2}\geq R^{2} (6.7)

for all z∈ℤn∖{0}z\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\setminus\{0\}. Moreover, it is clear that if ‖z‖≥R\norm{z}\geq R, then (6.7) holds. Hence it is enough to consider the zz such that 0<‖z‖<R0<\norm{z}<R, in which case (6.7) holds if and only if

|⟨u,z‖z‖⟩|≥(R2‖z‖2−1)1/2.\Biggl|\left\langle u,\frac{z}{\norm{z}}\right\rangle\Biggr|\geq\Bigl(\frac{R^{2}}{\norm{z}^{2}}-1\Bigr)^{1/2}. (6.8)

Since the right-hand side of equation (6.8) (call it θz\theta_{z}) is then nonnegative and z/‖z‖z/\norm{z} is unitary, we know by Lemma 2.5 (Bang’s lemma) that we can find a uu satisfying (6.8) of the form

u⁡(R)=12​∑0<‖z‖<Rϵz​θz​z‖z‖,u(R)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{0<\norm{z}<R}\epsilon_{z}\theta_{z}\frac{z}{\norm{z}},

where ϵz∈{±1}\epsilon_{z}\in\{\pm 1\} (the 1/21/2 factor comes from the fact that we apply Bang’s lemma with both choices of ±z/‖z‖\pm z/\norm{z} for every zz such that 0<‖z‖<R0<\norm{z}<R). Now that we know that ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} is admissible for ERE_{R} with this choice of u⁡(R)u(R), we have to show that (6.6) holds. Since the only unknown in this equation is now KK, we will try to estimate this value. We have

K=‖u‖=⟨u,u⟩=⟨u,v⟩K=\norm{u}=\sqrt{\left\langle u,u\right\rangle}=\left\langle u,v\right\rangle (6.9)

where v=u/‖u‖v=u/\norm{u}. By definition and linearity, this expression is

12​∑0<‖z‖<Rϵz​⟨z,v⟩‖z‖​θz≤12​∑0<‖z‖<R|⟨z,v⟩|‖z‖​(R2‖z‖2−1)1/2.\frac{1}{2}\sum_{0<\norm{z}<R}\epsilon_{z}\frac{\left\langle z,v\right\rangle}{\norm{z}}\theta_{z}\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{0<\norm{z}<R}\frac{\absolutevalue{\inner{z}{v}}}{\norm{z}}\Bigl(\frac{R^{2}}{\norm{z}^{2}}-1\Bigr)^{1/2}.

Call this last expression K′K^{\prime}.

The rest of the proof takes us too far afield from the usual plank problems arguments, but let us mention that Ball establishes that K′/RnK^{\prime}/R^{n} approximates a certain integral over the unit ball, and that in particular

K′Vol​(BR)→n2​(∫0π/2sinn−2​t​𝑑t)−1​∫0π/2cos⁡t​sinn−2​t​𝑑t​∫01(1−r2)1/2​rn−2​𝑑r.\frac{K^{\prime}}{\text{Vol}(B_{R})}\to\frac{n}{2}\Bigl(\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin^{n-2}t\,dt\Bigr)^{-1}\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos t\sin^{n-2}t\,dt\int_{0}^{1}(1-r^{2})^{1/2}r^{n-2}\,dr.

With an appropriate change of variables, we find

∫01(1−r2)1/2​rn−2​𝑑r=1n​∫0π/2sinn−2​t​𝑑t,\int_{0}^{1}(1-r^{2})^{1/2}r^{n-2}\,dr=\frac{1}{n}\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin^{n-2}t\,dt,

and so

K′Vol​(BR)→12​∫0π/2cos⁡t​sinn−2​t​𝑑t.\frac{K^{\prime}}{\text{Vol}(B_{R})}\to\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos t\sin^{n-2}t\,dt.

This last integral can be computed directly and equals (n−1)−1(n-1)^{-1}, proving (6.6). ∎
